### CVE-2024-6387: Qualys TRU & CISA — OpenSSH "regreSSHion": SIGALRM Async-Signal-Unsafe syslog() Heap RCE
- **ID:** `openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a bank accountant (sshd main thread) who is in the middle of erasing and rearranging pages inside the master ledger (glibc free()). Suddenly, a 120-second kitchen timer (LoginGraceTime SIGALRM) rings! The accountant freezes mid-sentence with the ledger pages half-torn, and an emergency clerk (grace_alarm_handler -> sigdie) rushes in to write a "Visitor Timed Out!" note in the logbook (syslog()). However, writing that note requires grabbing a brand-new 320-byte sheet of paper (fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320)) from the exact same half-torn ledger! By timing their packets to the microsecond, the attacker tricks the emergency clerk into grabbing a rigged page that redirects the bank’s instructions (_IO_wfile_jumps) to run the attacker’s code as root. Discovered by the Qualys Threat Research Unit (July 2024), "regreSSHion" (CVE-2024-6387) is an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in OpenSSH’s server (sshd versions 8.5p1–9.7p1) on glibc-based Linux systems. An accidental October 2020 refactoring removed #ifdef DO_LOG_SAFE_IN_SIGHAND from sigdie(), reintroducing a 2006 bug (CVE-2006-5051). When a client fails to log in within LoginGraceTime (120 seconds), sshd’s SIGALRM signal handler asynchronously calls syslog(), which invokes async-signal-unsafe glibc malloc()/free() routines, allowing an attacker who interrupts an in-progress free() call to corrupt glibc _IO_FILE vtable structures and gain root RCE.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: SSH HEAP GROOMING & LOGINGRACETIME EXPIRATION (T1190) -> Stage 2: SIGALRM INTERRUPTS FREE() & CALLS ASYNC-SIGNAL-UNSAFE SYSLOG() (T1068) -> Stage 3: GLIBC _IO_FILE VTABLE HIJACK & PRE-AUTH ROOT CODE EXECUTION (T1059.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU): regreSSHion: RCE in OpenSSH’s server, on glibc-based Linux systems (CVE-2024-6387)](https://www.qualys.com/2024/07/01/cve-2024-6387/regresshion.txt); [The OpenSSH Project: OpenSSH 9.8 Security Advisory: Async-Signal-Unsafe sigdie() Regression](https://www.openssh.com/txt/release-9.8); [CISA & Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: CVE-2024-6387 OpenSSH regreSSHion Detection & Mitigation Guidance](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/07/01/etr-openssh-remote-unauthenticated-code-execution-cve-2024-6387-regresshion/)

### CVE-2023-0669: Huntress, Mandiant & CISA — CL0P (TA505): Fortra GoAnywhere MFT LicenseServlet Deserialization RCE
- **ID:** `fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=fortra-goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-cl0p
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a software vault (GoAnywhere MFT) that has a special mail slot (/goanywhere/lic/accept) reserved for receiving encrypted license renewals from the manufacturer. To make sure only "official" license files are opened, the mail slot requires the package (bundle) to be locked with an AES cipher ($2). However, the developer hardcoded the exact AES password ("go@nywhereLicenseP@$$w0rd") right inside the public software binary that every customer downloads! Anyone who reads the binary can extract that password, lock a booby-trapped Java package (CommonsBeanutils1 gadget chain) with the official AES key, drop it into /goanywhere/lic/accept without logging in, and watch the server unlock and detonate it as SYSTEM. Synthesizing Horizon3.ai’s cryptographic root-cause analysis, Huntress Labs’ incident response forensics, and Mandiant / CISA advisories (February 2023), CVE-2023-0669 is the pre-authentication Java deserialization zero-day exploited by the CL0P ransomware group (TA505 / FIN11) against 130+ Fortra GoAnywhere MFT servers. Because LicenseResponseServlet (/goanywhere/lic/accept) decrypted incoming bundle parameters using a hardcoded static AES-128-CBC key and passed the plaintext directly to ObjectInputStream.readObject(), attackers sent a ysoserial CommonsBeanutils1 gadget chain to execute SYSTEM commands and deploy TrueBot and Cobalt Strike.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: ENCRYPTED BUNDLE POST TO /GOANYWHERE/LIC/ACCEPT (CVE-2023-0669) (T1190) -> Stage 2: COMMONSBEANUTILS1 GADGET DESERIALIZATION & SYSTEM SHELL (T1059.003) -> Stage 3: TRUEBOT / COBALT STRIKE DEPLOYMENT & MFT VAULT EXFILTRATION (T1219)
- **Primary Sources:** [Horizon3.ai Attack Team: GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2023-0669 Pre-Auth RCE Technical Deep Dive](https://www.horizon3.ai/attack-research/attack-blogs/goanywhere-mft-cve-2023-0669-deep-dive-and-indicators-of-compromise/); [Huntress Security Research: Investigating GoAnywhere MFT RCE (CVE-2023-0669) Exploitation & Stack Traces](https://www.huntress.com/blog/investigating-goanywhere-mft-rce-cve-2023-0669); [Mandiant & CISA KEV: FIN11 / CL0P Exploitation of GoAnywhere MFT Zero-Day Deploying TrueBot & Cobalt Strike](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)

### CVE-2023-29059: CrowdStrike, Kaspersky & Mandiant — Lazarus (SmoothOperator): 3CXDesktopApp Supply Chain & Gopuram
- **ID:** `3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=3cx-desktopapp-supply-chain-lazarus
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a thief (Lazarus Group) who wants to break into a corporate phone system company (3CX). First, they poison an older trading program (X_TRADER) that a 3CX software engineer happens to install on their computer; that gives the thief access to 3CX’s official software factory! Inside the factory, the thief swaps out one helper library (ffmpeg.dll) inside the official 3CXDesktopApp installer before the factory stamps its genuine digital signature on the package. When thousands of companies install the update, 3CXDesktopApp.exe loads the rigged ffmpeg.dll, which reads secret encrypted instructions hidden after a 0xFEEDFACE bookmark inside a neighbor file (d3dcompiler_47.dll), checks innocent-looking icon files (icon1.ico) on GitHub to find the active command server, and steals browser passwords (ICONICSTEALER) or plants the Gopuram spyware! Synthesizing CrowdStrike (Labyrinth Chollima), Kaspersky GReAT (Gopuram), and Mandiant (UNC4736) analyses (March–April 2023), CVE-2023-29059 ("SmoothOperator") is a cascading supply chain compromise where North Korean threat actors trojanized the official Windows and macOS builds of 3CXDesktopApp (versions 18.12.407 and 18.12.416). When the validly signed 3CXDesktopApp.exe starts, it sideloads a trojanized ffmpeg.dll, which reads an RC4-encrypted shellcode blob embedded after marker 0xFEEDFACE inside d3dcompiler_47.dll, fetches AES-encrypted C2 URLs appended to .ico files on GitHub (IconStorages), and deploys ICONICSTEALER or the Gopuram backdoor in memory.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: TROJANIZED FFMPEG.DLL SIDE-LOADING & 0xFEEDFACE RC4 DECRYPTION (T1195.002) -> Stage 2: GITHUB ICON1.ICO DEAD-DROP RESOLVER & AES-GCM C2 EXTRACTION (T1102.001) -> Stage 3: IN-MEMORY ICONICSTEALER & KASPERSKY GOPURAM BACKDOOR DEPLOYMENT (T1555.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [CrowdStrike Falcon OverWatch & Threat Intelligence: CrowdStrike Detects and Prevents Active Intrusion Campaign Targeting 3CXDesktopApp Customers](https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/crowdstrike-detects-and-prevents-active-intrusion-campaign-targeting-3cxdesktopapp-customers/); [Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): 3CX Software Supply Chain Compromise Initiated by a Prior Software Supply Chain Compromise (UNC4736)](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): Not just an infostealer: Gopuram backdoor deployed through 3CX supply chain attack](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)

### CVE-2021-42287: Microsoft, CrowdStrike & Splunk — Active Directory "noPac": sAMAccountName Spoofing & KDC Impersonation
- **ID:** `nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an office building where any regular employee is allowed to register up to 10 company laptops (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10). Normally, every laptop nametag must end with a $ symbol (FAKEPC01$). However, the badge clerk (CVE-2021-42278) forgets to check for the $ when someone renames a laptop! So the employee renames their laptop to CORP-DC01 (the exact name of the Chief Security Officer’s vault computer, minus the $), grabs a temporary lobby ticket (TGT), and immediately renames their laptop back to FAKEPC01$. Next, they hand that CORP-DC01 lobby ticket to the inner vault desk (KDC S4U2self) and ask for an Admin pass. When the vault clerk looks up CORP-DC01 and sees it no longer exists, the clerk has a quirky habit (CVE-2021-42287): "Let me add a $ to the end and check again!" Adding $ matches the real Chief Security Officer’s vault (CORP-DC01$), so the clerk prints a full Domain Admin master key for the real Domain Controller! Synthesizing Microsoft MSRC advisories, CrowdStrike Falcon Threat Intelligence, and Splunk SURGe detection research (November–December 2021), "noPac" chains two Active Directory flaws, CVE-2021-42278 (sAMAccountName spoofing) and CVE-2021-42287 (KDC $ fallback), to elevate any low-privilege domain user to Domain Administrator in seconds. The attacker creates a machine account via ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota, renames its sAMAccountName to match a Domain Controller without the trailing $, requests a Kerberos TGT, renames the account back, and uses S4U2self to trick the KDC into issuing a Domain Admin service ticket encrypted for the real CORP-DC01$ Domain Controller.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: MACHINE ACCOUNT CREATION & SAMACCOUNTNAME SPOOFING (CVE-2021-42278) (T1068) -> Stage 2: RENAME BACK & KDC S4U2SELF "$" FALLBACK (CVE-2021-42287) (T1558.001) -> Stage 3: DOMAIN CONTROLLER IMPERSONATION & NTDS.DIT DCSYNC (T1003.006)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): Active Directory sAMAccountName Spoofing (CVE-2021-42278) & KDC Pac Bypass (CVE-2021-42287)](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-42287); [CrowdStrike Threat Intelligence: Understanding the Active Directory SamAccountName Spoofing / noPac Exploitation Chain](https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/); [Splunk SURGe Security Research: Detecting Active Directory noPac (CVE-2021-42278 & CVE-2021-42287) with EventID 4741 and 4781](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/)

### CVE-2020-1472: Secura, CISA & CrowdStrike — Active Directory "Zerologon": Netlogon AES-CFB8 All-Zero IV Takeover
- **ID:** `zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a high-security vault door (Netlogon MS-NRPC) where the guard tests visitors by handing them a secret key calculator (AES-CFB8). Normally, scrambling an 8-digit number with a secret key produces a completely unpredictable 8-digit answer. However, the engineer who built the calculator made a fatal mistake: they wired the starting dial (Initialization Vector / IV) permanently to 0000000000000000! Because of how AES-CFB8 math works when the starting dial is all zeroes, if a visitor types in 00000000 as their challenge, there is an exact 1-in-256 chance that the encrypted answer is ALSO 00000000, no matter what the Domain Controller’s secret password is! By knocking on the door ~256 times in 3 seconds with all zeroes, the attacker gets waved right in and resets the Domain Controller’s own password to blank. Discovered by Tom Tervoort of Secura and mandated for emergency patching under CISA Emergency Directive 20-04 (August–September 2020), "Zerologon" (CVE-2020-1472, CVSS 10.0) is a catastrophic cryptographic flaw in the Windows Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC). Because ComputeNetlogonCredential() used AES-CFB8 with a fixed all-zero 16-byte IV, supplying an 8-byte client challenge of all zeroes (0x00*8) yields an all-zero credential for 1 out of every 256 random session keys. In ~3 seconds without any domain credentials, an attacker bypasses NetrServerAuthenticate3, calls NetrServerPasswordSet2 to overwrite the Domain Controller’s CORP-DC01$ machine password with an empty string (EventID 4742), and dumps NTDS.dit via DCSync.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: ALL-ZERO AES-CFB8 CHALLENGE SPOOFING (CVE-2020-1472) (T1210) -> Stage 2: OVERWRITING THE DOMAIN CONTROLLER PASSWORD VIA NETRSERVERPASSWORDSET2 (T1098) -> Stage 3: DCSYNC DOMAIN DUMP & REGISTRY MACHINE PASSWORD RESTORATION (T1003.006)
- **Primary Sources:** [Secura BV (Tom Tervoort): Zerologon: Unauthenticated Domain Controller Compromise by Subverting Netlogon Cryptography (CVE-2020-1472)](https://www.secura.com/blog/zero-logon); [Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA): Emergency Directive 20-04: Mitigate Netlogon Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability from August 2020 Patch Tuesday](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-20-04-mitigate-netlogon-elevation-privilege-vulnerability-august-2020-patch); [Microsoft Threat Intelligence & CrowdStrike: Detecting CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) via Windows EventID 5805, 4742 & Netlogon RPC Inspection](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2020/09/28/new-detections-for-cve-2020-1472-active-exploitation/)

### CVE-2021-34473: DEVCORE, Mandiant & CISA — Microsoft Exchange "ProxyShell": Autodiscover SSRF to MailboxExport Webshell
- **ID:** `proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a corporate mailroom (Exchange Client Access Frontend :443) where a receptionist is trained to help people find their mailbox settings (/autodiscover/autodiscover.json). If someone writes /autodiscover/autodiscover.json/alice@corp.com/settings, the receptionist crosses out /autodiscover/autodiscover.json/alice@corp.com and forwards /settings to the high-security back office (Exchange Backend :444) stamped with the building’s master SYSTEM seal. Orange Tsai discovered that if you request /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/, the receptionist gets confused by the ?@, crosses out /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com, and forwards /powershell/ straight into the restricted Admin PowerShell room! Once inside, you hand the clerk a forged ID card (X-Rps-CAT), grant yourself "Mailbox Export" rights, and export a booby-trapped email directly into the public web folder as shell.aspx! Discovered by Orange Tsai of DEVCORE (Pwn2Own 2021) and documented by Joint CISA Advisory AA21-265A, Mandiant, and Splunk SURGe, "ProxyShell" chains three Microsoft Exchange vulnerabilities into a 1-click unauthenticated SYSTEM RCE: (1) CVE-2021-34473 (pre-auth URL path confusion via /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/ to reach the backend PowerShell endpoint as SYSTEM), (2) CVE-2021-34523 (X-Rps-CAT token deserialization to impersonate the Exchange Administrator), and (3) CVE-2021-31207 (New-MailboxExportRequest arbitrary file write to drop a polyglot .pst/.aspx webshell into C:\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: AUTODISCOVER.JSON PATH CONFUSION & ACL BYPASS (CVE-2021-34473) (T1190) -> Stage 2: POWERSHELL X-RPS-CAT IMPERSONATION & ROLE ASSIGNMENT (CVE-2021-34523) (T1059.001) -> Stage 3: NEW-MAILBOXEXPORTREQUEST ARBITRARY .ASPX WEBSHELL WRITE (CVE-2021-31207) (T1505.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [DEVCORE Security Research (Orange Tsai): ProxyShell: A New Attack Surface on MS Exchange Part 3 (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207)](https://devco.re/blog/2021/08/06/a-new-attack-surface-on-ms-exchange-part-3-ProxyShell/); [CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: Exploitation of Microsoft Exchange Server Vulnerabilities (ProxyShell)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2021/08/21/cisa-and-fbi-release-advisory-conti-ransomware-and-proxyshell); [Huntress Labs & Mandiant: Incident Response Analysis: Detecting ProxyShell Exploitation & MailboxExportRequest Webshells](https://www.huntress.com/blog/)

### CVE-2021-34527: Microsoft, Rapid7 & Elastic — Windows "PrintNightmare": RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Remote SYSTEM RCE
- **ID:** `printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527
- **Category:** ACTIVE_DIRECTORY | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a corporate print room (spoolsv.exe, running as SYSTEM on every Windows server and Domain Controller) where only IT Administrators are supposed to install new printer driver software (ValidateObjectAccess). However, the rulebook for the RpcAddPrinterDriverEx command has a bizarre loophole written in the fine print: "If the caller checks the 0x8000 box (APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER), skip the ID check!" By checking that 0x8000 box and telling the Print Spooler that the printer’s "configuration helper file" (pConfigFile) is sitting on the attacker’s own shared folder (\\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll), any regular employee can trick a Domain Controller’s Print Spooler into downloading and running evil.dll as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM! Synthesizing Microsoft MSRC advisories, Rapid7’s RPC reverse engineering, and Elastic Security Labs’ telemetry analysis (June–July 2021), "PrintNightmare" (CVE-2021-34527 / CVE-2021-1675) is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the Windows Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe). By calling RpcAddPrinterDriverEx() over \pipe\spoolss (MS-RPRN) or RpcAsyncAddPrinterDriver() (MS-PAR) with bit 0x8000 (APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER) set in dwFileCopyFlags, any authenticated domain user bypasses ValidateObjectAccess() and forces the remote server’s spoolsv.exe (SYSTEM) to copy and LoadLibraryW() an arbitrary DLL from an attacker-controlled UNC share.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: RPCADDPRINTERDRIVEREX AUTH BYPASS VIA 0x8000 FLAG (CVE-2021-34527) (T1210) -> Stage 2: UNC DRIVER COPY & SYSTEM DLL LOAD IN SPOOLSV.EXE (T1547.012) -> Stage 3: DLLMAIN SYSTEM EXECUTION & DOMAIN CONTROLLER COMPROMISE (T1068)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC): Windows Print Spooler Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2021-34527 / PrintNightmare)](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-34527); [Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527): Technical Analysis of MS-RPRN RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Exploitation](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2021/06/30/printnightmare-cve-2021-1675-remote-code-execution-in-windows-spooler-service/); [Elastic Security Labs & CISA: Detecting PrintNightmare via PrintService Operational EventID 316 and Sysmon EventID 7/11](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2021/06/30/printnightmare-critical-windows-print-spooler-vulnerability)

### CVE-2023-29357: STAR Labs, Rapid7 & CISA — Microsoft SharePoint: JWT "alg:none" Auth Bypass to BCS RCE Chain
- **ID:** `sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a VIP corporate portal (SharePoint Server) that accepts digital passports (OAuth2 JSON Web Tokens / JWT). Every passport has a top section (Header) that tells the guard which cryptographic signature pen was used to sign it (RS256), and a bottom section (Signature). At Pwn2Own 2023, STAR Labs discovered that if you print a fake passport whose top section says "alg": "none" ("No signature pen used!") and leave the signature blank, the SharePoint guard (SPJsonWebSecurityBaseTokenHandler) says: "Well, since it says none, I don’t need to check a signature, welcome in, Farm Administrator!" Once inside as the Farm Admin, the attacker imports a custom "Business Data Connector" (.bdcm file) containing a compiled C# program (DotNetAssembly) that SharePoint loads straight into memory! Discovered by Nguyễn Tiến Giang (Jang) of STAR Labs at Pwn2Own Vancouver 2023 and documented by Microsoft MSRC, Rapid7, and CISA KEV, this scenario chains two flaws in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server: (1) CVE-2023-29357 (CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication privilege escalation via unsigned "alg": "none" OAuth2 JSON Web Tokens) and (2) CVE-2023-24955 (authenticated Remote Code Execution via Business Connectivity Services .bdcm DotNetAssembly loading inside w3wp.exe).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: FORGING AN UNSIGNED OAUTH JWT WITH "ALG: NONE" (CVE-2023-29357) (T1190) -> Stage 2: IMPERSONATING THE SHAREPOINT FARM ADMINISTRATOR (T1550.001) -> Stage 3: BUSINESS CONNECTIVITY SERVICES (.BDCM) ASSEMBLY RCE (CVE-2023-24955) (T1505.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [STAR Labs SG (Nguyễn Tiến Giang): SharePoint Pre-Auth RCE Chain (CVE-2023-29357 & CVE-2023-24955) Technical Writeup](https://starlabs.sg/blog/2023/09-sharepoint-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2023-29357-and-cve-2023-24955/); [Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Analysis of SharePoint Server Elevation of Privilege (CVE-2023-29357)](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/); [Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV: Microsoft SharePoint Server Elevation of Privilege & RCE Advisories (CVE-2023-29357 / CVE-2023-24955)](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-29357)

### CVE-2023-34048: Mandiant, VMware & CISA — UNC3886: vCenter vmdird Out-of-Bounds Write & ESXi VIRTUALPITA Backdoor
- **ID:** `vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a master control tower (VMware vCenter Server) that holds the master skeleton keys (vpxuser) to every apartment building (ESXi Hypervisor) in a city. Most companies put security guards (EDR agents) inside the individual apartments (Windows/Linux Guest VMs), but cannot install a guard inside the concrete foundation of the apartment building itself (ESXi Hypervisor). For two years, the espionage group UNC3886 used a zero-day flaw (CVE-2023-34048) in the control tower’s directory phone line (vmdird DCERPC) to break into vCenter, unlocked the master key safe (symkey.dat + VPX_HOST), and planted secret maintenance hatches (VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE) in the concrete foundation of every ESXi building, using internal dumbwaiter shafts (AF_VSOCK sockets) to move silently into any apartment without ever stepping out onto the street where network cameras (Firewalls / NDR) could see them! Synthesizing Mandiant (Google Cloud) threat intelligence on UNC3886, VMware Advisory VMSA-2023-0023, and CISA KEV (October 2023–June 2024), this scenario traces how UNC3886 exploited CVE-2023-34048 (CVSS 9.8 out-of-bounds heap write in vmdird DCERPC) as a zero-day for over two years. After achieving root RCE on vCenter and wiping /var/core/core.vmdird.* crash dumps, the attacker extracts and decrypts vpxuser service credentials from the VCDB PostgreSQL database using /etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat, lowers ESXi VIB acceptance levels, and deploys the VIRTUALPITA and VIRTUALPIE backdoors communicating over AF_VSOCK (VMCI) sockets.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: VCENTER VMDIRD DCERPC OUT-OF-BOUNDS WRITE (CVE-2023-34048) (T1190) -> Stage 2: EXTRACTING & DECRYPTING ESXI "VPXUSER" CREDENTIALS FROM VCDB (T1552.001) -> Stage 3: DEPLOYING VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE VIB BACKDOORS OVER AF_VSOCK (T1547)
- **Primary Sources:** [Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): Cloaked and Covert: Uncovering UNC3886 Espionage Operations on VMware vCenter & ESXi (CVE-2023-34048)](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/uncovering-unc3886-espionage-operations); [VMware / Broadcom Security Response: VMSA-2023-0023: VMware vCenter Server Out-of-Bounds Write Vulnerability (CVE-2023-34048)](https://support.broadcom.com/web/ecx/support-content-notification/-/external/content/SecurityAdvisories/0/23254); [Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA): CISA Adds VMware vCenter CVE-2023-34048 to Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)

### CVE-2023-2868: Mandiant & CISA — UNC4841: Barracuda ESG .tar Command Injection, SALTWATER & SEASPY Backdoors
- **ID:** `barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a corporate mail-screening machine (Barracuda Email Security Gateway) that opens every incoming .tar package before the recipient even sees the email, and writes down the name of each file inside on a Perl clipboard (qx/file '$filename'/). The espionage group UNC4841 mailed a .tar package where the file’s name itself was written as '|sh -c "curl ..."! The moment the screening machine read the label out loud, it executed the shell command as root. Once inside, UNC4841 welded a secret wiretap into the mail room’s main door (SALTWATER in bsmtp), hid a silent radio listener on the network cable (SEASPY using libpcap), and booby-trapped the building’s SQLite database (SUBMARINE) so deeply that Barracuda and CISA told every victim: "Throw the entire appliance in the trash and get a brand-new one!" Synthesizing Mandiant’s UNC4841 investigation, CISA Malware Analysis Reports (MAR-10454006), and Barracuda security advisories (May–August 2023), CVE-2023-2868 (CVSS 9.8) is a zero-click unauthenticated command injection flaw in Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances (v5.1.3–9.2.0). Sending an inbound SMTP email with a crafted .tar attachment whose member filename starts with '| triggers root command execution inside the Perl attachment scanner, deploying the SALTWATER (/usr/sbin/bsmtp), SEASPY (libpcap passive backdoor), and SUBMARINE (SQLite trigger) implants.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: MALICIOUS .TAR ATTACHMENT FILENAME INJECTION (CVE-2023-2868) (T1190) -> Stage 2: IMPLANTING "SALTWATER" (BSMTP) & "SEASPY" (PCAP SNIFFER) (T1505.003) -> Stage 3: DEEP PERSISTENCE VIA "SUBMARINE" & EMAIL SPOOL EXFILTRATION (T1114.002)
- **Primary Sources:** [Mandiant Threat Intelligence (Google Cloud): Barracuda ESG Zero-Day Vulnerability (CVE-2023-2868) Exploited Globally by Aggressive Espionage Actor UNC4841](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally); [CISA & FBI Malware Analysis Report: MAR-10454006: CISA Releases Malware Analysis Reports on Barracuda Backdoors (SUBMARINE, WHIRLPOOL, SALTWATER)](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2023/07/28/cisa-releases-malware-analysis-report-submarine-malware-used-barracuda-esg-exploit); [Barracuda Networks Trust Center: Barracuda Email Security Gateway Appliance (ESG) Vulnerability CVE-2023-2868 Incident Notice](https://www.barracuda.com/company/legal/esg-vulnerability)

### CVE-2023-20198: Cisco Talos, VulnCheck & CISA — Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Chain & "BadCandy" Lua Implant
- **ID:** `cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a building where the front-door guard (NGINX Reverse Proxy) has strict orders: "Block any stranger who asks to visit room /webui_wsma_http!" However, the attacker writes the room name on their visitor slip using a double-layered cipher (/%2577ebui_wsma_http, where %2577 is %77 encoded twice). The front-door guard decodes the first layer (/%77ebui_wsma_http), says "Well, that doesn’t spell /webui_wsma_http!", and waves the slip through to the back-office clerk (WSMA Backend). The back-office clerk decodes the second layer (%77 -> w), sees /webui_wsma_http, and dutifully creates a master privilege 15 administrator account (CVE-2023-20198)! Next, using that new account, the attacker exploits a second bug (CVE-2023-20273) to break out into the router’s underlying Linux room, plants the BadCandy Lua spy script inside NGINX’s memory, and erases the temporary admin account so the router’s configuration looks 100% clean! Discovered and analyzed by Cisco Talos, VulnCheck, and CISA (October 2023), this two-zero-day chain compromised over 40,000 internet-facing Cisco IOS XE routers and switches with the Web UI enabled. First, requesting /%2577ebui_wsma_http (CVE-2023-20198, CVSS 10.0) bypasses NGINX authentication checks to reach the internal WSMA SOAP handler and create a local privilege 15 administrator account. Second, authenticating with that account to /webui/rest/softwareMgmt/installAdd (CVE-2023-20273) injects commands as Linux root to implant the BadCandy Lua webshell (/usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf -> oregon_http.lua) inside NGINX.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: DOUBLE URL-ENCODING BYPASS ON /%2577EBUI_WSMA_HTTP (CVE-2023-20198) (T1190) -> Stage 2: INSTALLADD COMMAND INJECTION TO LINUX ROOT (CVE-2023-20273) (T1068) -> Stage 3: IMPLANTING THE "BADCANDY" LUA WEBSHELL IN NGINX (T1505.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [Cisco Talos Intelligence Group: Active Exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface (CVE-2023-20198 & CVE-2023-20273)](https://blog.talosintelligence.com/active-exploitation-of-cisco-ios-xe-software/); [VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence: Cisco IOS XE CVE-2023-20198 Deep Dive: NGINX /%2577ebui_wsma_http Double URL-Encoding Bypass](https://vulncheck.com/blog/cisco-ios-xe); [CISA & Cisco PSIRT: CISA Releases Guidance on Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Exploitation](https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-iosxe-webui-privesc-j22SaA4z)

### CVE-2023-28771: TRAPA Security, Rapid7 & CISA — Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth IKEv2 Packet Decoder Command Injection
- **ID:** `zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a castle gatekeeper (Zyxel ssod IKEv2 VPN Daemon on UDP port 500) who receives an error note (Notify Payload Type 14) from a stranger outside the moat. The first 48 letters of the note are locked with a secret cipher (3DES-CBC), but the gatekeeper’s cipher key is printed right inside the public instruction manual! Even worse, once the gatekeeper unlocks those first 48 letters, they don’t even check if the rest of the note was locked, and to record the error in their diary (/tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log), they shout to a root servant (system()): echo "<Stranger’s Note>" >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log! By writing "; curl http://.../z.sh | sh ; echo " at the end of the UDP packet, the stranger takes over the entire firewall with a single UDP packet! Discovered by TRAPA Security and analyzed by Rapid7 and CISA KEV (April–May 2023), CVE-2023-28771 (CVSS 9.8) is an unauthenticated remote OS command injection flaw in the IKEv2 VPN daemon (/usr/sbin/ssod) of Zyxel ATP, USG FLEX, VPN, and ZyWALL firewalls. When an attacker sends a single UDP packet to port 500 containing an IKE_SA_INIT Notify payload (type 14), libike.so decrypts the first 48 bytes using a hardcoded 3DES key and passes the unescaped payload string directly into system("echo ... >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log") as root.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: CRAFTING AN IKEV2 NOTIFY PAYLOAD WITH ZYXEL’S HARDCODED 3DES KEY (CVE-2023-28771) (T1190) -> Stage 2: BREAKING OUT OF SYSTEM("ECHO ... >> /TMP/SDWAN_VPNDEBUG.LOG") (T1059.004) -> Stage 3: PERIMETER FIREWALL TAKEOVER & INTERNAL LAN PIVOTING (T1583.005)
- **Primary Sources:** [TRAPA Security Research: Root Cause Analysis of Zyxel Firewall Unauthenticated Remote Command Execution (CVE-2023-28771)](https://trapa.security/blog/cve-2023-28771/); [Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth Command Injection (CVE-2023-28771) Exploit & Network Signatures](https://attackerkb.com/topics/N3i8dxpFKS/cve-2023-28771/rapid7-analysis); [Zyxel PSIRT & CISA KEV: Zyxel Security Advisory for OS Command Injection Vulnerability in Firewalls (CVE-2023-28771)](https://www.zyxel.com/global/en/support/security-advisories/zyxel-security-advisory-for-remote-command-injection-vulnerability-of-firewalls)

### CVE-2023-36845: watchTowr, VulnCheck & CISA — Juniper Junos OS J-Web: PHPRC "/dev/fd/0" Fileless Pre-Auth RCE
- **ID:** `juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a chef (FreeBSD php-cgi) who starts work every morning by reading a rulebook (php.ini) from a shelf whose location is written on a sticky note (PHPRC environment variable). In Juniper’s J-Web kitchen (Appweb), any visitor walking up to /webauth_operation.php is accidentally allowed to rewrite that sticky note (?PHPRC=..., CVE-2023-36845)! At first, researchers thought you had to smuggle a fake rulebook onto a shelf inside the kitchen first (CVE-2023-36846). Then VulnCheck realized something brilliant: what if you write PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 on the sticky note, telling the chef that the rulebook is the visitor’s own order slip (Standard Input / HTTP POST Body)? The chef reads the visitor’s POST body as php.ini, sees the rule auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...", and runs the visitor’s PHP code in memory without touching a single file on disk! Synthesizing watchTowr Labs’ initial J-Web exploit chain, VulnCheck’s single-request fileless refinement, and Juniper SIRT Advisory JSA72300 / CISA KEV (August 2023), CVE-2023-36845 allows an unauthenticated attacker to manipulate the PHPRC environment variable on Juniper SRX firewalls and EX switches. By sending POST /webauth_operation.php?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 with an HTTP request body containing allow_url_include=1 and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...", the FreeBSD php-cgi process parses the HTTP POST body (stdin / /dev/fd/0) as php.ini and executes arbitrary PHP and shell commands completely filelessly.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: MANIPULATING THE "PHPRC" ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE VIA J-WEB (CVE-2023-36845) (T1190) -> Stage 2: INJECTING AUTO_PREPEND_FILE="DATA://..." IN THE HTTP POST BODY (T1574.007) -> Stage 3: FILELESS IN-MEMORY PHP EXECUTION & JUNOS CONFIG EXTRACTION (T1059.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [watchTowr Labs: CVEs-2023-36844 to 36847: Juniper SRX & EX Pre-Auth Remote Code Execution Chain](https://labs.watchtowr.com/cve-2023-36844-and-friends-rce-in-juniper-firewalls/); [VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence: Single-Request Fileless RCE on Juniper J-Web via PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 (CVE-2023-36845)](https://vulncheck.com/blog/juniper-cve-2023-36845); [Juniper SIRT & CISA KEV: 2023-08 Out-of-Cycle Security Bulletin: Junos OS SRX and EX Series J-Web Vulnerabilities (JSA72300)](https://supportportal.juniper.net/s/article/2023-08-Out-of-Cycle-Security-Bulletin-Junos-OS-SRX-Series-and-EX-Series-Multiple-vulnerabilities-in-J-Web-can-be-combined-to-allow-a-preAuth-Remote-Code-Execution)

### CVE-2023-22515: Microsoft, Rapid7 & CISA — Storm-0062: Atlassian Confluence XWork OGNL Setup Reset & OSGi Webshell
- **ID:** `atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=atlassian-confluence-cve-2023-22515-storm0062
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a commercial bank vault (Atlassian Confluence) that has a special "First-Day Factory Setup Mode" (setupComplete=false) used only on the day the vault is installed so the builder can register the first master manager. Once installation finishes, a latch flips to setupComplete=true and locks the setup screen forever. However, the public lobby clock (/server-info.action) is wired to the bank’s internal control board through Apache XWork parameter chains. By adding ?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false to a lobby clock query, Storm-0062 reaches through the wiring, flips the factory latch back to false, walks into the newly unlocked setup room (/setup/setupadministrator.action) to print a master admin badge, and flips the latch back to true so nobody notices! Synthesizing Microsoft Threat Intelligence (Storm-0062 / DarkShadow), Rapid7, Atlassian, and Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-289A (October 2023), CVE-2023-22515 (CVSS 10.0) is a zero-day Broken Access Control / XWork parameter injection vulnerability in Atlassian Confluence Data Center and Server (8.0.0–8.5.1). An unauthenticated attacker sends an HTTP request to /server-info.action?bootstrapStatusProvider.applicationConfig.setupComplete=false to reset the server’s installation state in memory, submits /setup/setupadministrator.action with X-Atlassian-Token: no-check to create a rogue confluence-administrators account, calls /setup/finishsetup.action to restore normal UI behavior, and uploads a malicious OSGi servlet plugin (.jar) via /rest/plugins/1.0/ for full OS command execution.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: XWork Parameter Injection (/server-info.action setupComplete=false) (T1190) -> Stage 2: Rogue Admin Provisioning (/setup/setupadministrator.action) (T1136.001) -> Stage 3: Malicious OSGi Plugin Upload & JVM Shell Execution (T1505.003)
- **Primary Sources:** [CISA, FBI & MS-ISAC Joint Advisory: AA23-289A: Threat Actors Exploit Atlassian Confluence CVE-2023-22515 for Initial Access](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-289a); [Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Atlassian Confluence Zero-Day Broken Access Control (CVE-2023-22515) Technical Analysis](https://attackerkb.com/topics/Q5f0ItSzw5/cve-2023-22515/rapid7-analysis); [Atlassian Security & Microsoft Threat Intelligence: Confluence Data Center and Server Broken Access Control Vulnerability (CVE-2023-22515)](https://confluence.atlassian.com/security/cve-2023-22515-broken-access-control-vulnerability-in-confluence-data-center-and-server-1295682276.html)

### CVE-2023-46604: Rapid7, Huntress & Trend Micro — Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire ExceptionResponse Deserialization RCE
- **ID:** `apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a message-sorting warehouse (Apache ActiveMQ) where delivery trucks communicate over TCP port 61616 using a binary walkie-talkie protocol called OpenWire. Whenever a truck encounters an error, it sends an "Exception Report" (Command Type 31: ExceptionResponse) listing the Java error class name and a message string so the warehouse computer can recreate the error object in memory (Class.forName(className).getConstructor(String.class).newInstance(message)). However, the warehouse computer forgets to check whether the named class is actually an Error class! The attacker sends an Exception Report naming Spring’s ClassPathXmlApplicationContext as the "error class" and a URL to a malicious poc.xml file as the "error message", causing the warehouse computer to download the XML blueprint and immediately run the attacker’s shell commands! Synthesizing Rapid7, Huntress Labs, Trend Micro, and CISA KEV (October–November 2023), CVE-2023-46604 (CVSS 10.0) is an unauthenticated Remote Code Execution vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ’s OpenWire protocol marshaller on TCP port 61616. By sending a crafted ExceptionResponse frame (data structure type 31 / 0x1F), an attacker forces BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable() to instantiate org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext with an attacker-controlled HTTP URL, causing the ActiveMQ JVM to fetch a remote Spring XML configuration and execute OS commands via java.lang.ProcessBuilder.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: OpenWire ExceptionResponse (0x1F) Arbitrary Class Instantiation (T1190) -> Stage 2: createThrowable() Reflection & Remote Spring XML Fetch (T1203) -> Stage 3: Spring ProcessBuilder init-method="start" RCE (T1059.004)
- **Primary Sources:** [Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response: Suspected Ransomware Activity Targeting Apache ActiveMQ (CVE-2023-46604)](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/11/01/etr-suspected-ransomware-activity-targeting-apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604/); [Huntress Security Research: Active Exploitation of Apache ActiveMQ CVE-2023-46604 in the Wild](https://www.huntress.com/blog/active-exploitation-of-apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604); [Apache Software Foundation & Trend Micro: Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire Unauthenticated RCE Advisory (CVE-2023-46604)](https://activemq.apache.org/security-advisories.data/CVE-2023-46604-announcement.txt)

### CVE-2023-27350: Horizon3.ai, CISA & Microsoft — PaperCut MF/NG SetupCompleted Auth Bypass & Rhino JS SYSTEM RCE
- **ID:** `papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=papercut-ng-cve-2023-27350-bl00dy
- **Category:** NETWORK_WEB | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a corporate print-management building (PaperCut MF/NG) where the "Welcome / Setup Completed" reception page (/app?service=page/SetupCompleted) was left unlocked years after the building opened. Even worse, clicking the "Login" button on that welcome page doesn’t ask for a password, it tells the security desk to automatically sign the visitor in as the master admin (performLogin("admin"))! Once handed the master admin cookie, the attacker walks into the printer scripting room, turns off the JavaScript safety cage (print.script.sandboxed=N), and writes a one-line printer script (java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)) that runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM the instant they click Save. Synthesizing Horizon3.ai’s root-cause analysis, Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-131A, and Microsoft Threat Intelligence (April–May 2023), CVE-2023-27350 (CVSS 9.8) is an unauthenticated session-hijacking and Remote Code Execution flaw in PaperCut MF and NG exploited by the Bl00dy Ransomware Gang, Cl0p, and LockBit. An unauthenticated attacker visits /app?service=page/SetupCompleted and submits the Login form listener to mint an authenticated admin JSESSIONID cookie, disables the Rhino JavaScript sandbox (print.script.sandboxed=N) in ConfigEditor, and injects java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec() into a Printer Script running inside pc-app.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: Tapestry SetupCompleted Authentication Bypass (performLogin) (T1190) -> Stage 2: Disabling Print Script Sandbox (print.script.sandboxed=N) (T1059.007) -> Stage 3: Rhino JS Runtime.getRuntime().exec() as SYSTEM (pc-app.exe) (T1059.001)
- **Primary Sources:** [CISA & FBI Joint Advisory: AA23-131A: Malicious Actors Exploit CVE-2023-27350 in PaperCut MF and NG](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-131a); [Horizon3.ai Attack Team: PaperCut CVE-2023-27350 Deep Dive and Indicators of Compromise](https://www.horizon3.ai/attack-research/attack-blogs/papercut-cve-2023-27350-deep-dive-and-indicators-of-compromise/); [PaperCut Software & Microsoft Threat Intelligence: PaperCut MF/NG Security Bulletin (March/April 2023) — CVE-2023-27350 & CVE-2023-27351](https://www.papercut.com/kb/Main/PO-1216-and-PO-1219)

### CVE-2022-42821: Microsoft Threat Intel & Jamf — macOS Gatekeeper "Achilles" Bypass via AppleDouble Restrictive ACLs
- **ID:** `macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** HIGH
- **Overview:** Imagine an airport customs checkpoint (macOS Gatekeeper) that only inspects suitcases that have a bright red "ARRIVED FROM OVERSEAS" sticker (com.apple.quarantine extended attribute) pasted on them by the baggage handler (Safari) the moment they come off the plane. If a suitcase has no red sticker, customs assumes it belongs to a local airport worker and waves it straight through without opening it. In the "Achilles" attack, the smuggler packs their suitcase (Update.app) inside a shipping crate (Update.zip) alongside a special macOS instruction sheet (._Update.app AppleDouble file) that coats the suitcase in Teflon (NFSv4 ACL: deny writeextattr). When Safari unpacks the crate and tries to stick the red com.apple.quarantine label onto the suitcase, the Teflon ACL makes the sticker slide right off (EACCES), so Gatekeeper waves the unsigned malware straight through with zero warnings! Discovered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence researcher Jonathan Bar Or and analyzed with Jamf Threat Labs (December 2022), CVE-2022-42821 ("Achilles") is a logic vulnerability in macOS Gatekeeper and Lockdown Mode. By packaging an unsigned .app bundle inside a ZIP archive alongside an AppleDouble metadata file (._Update.app) carrying an NFSv4 Access Control List (com.apple.acl.text) that denies writeextattr permissions to everyone, the attacker causes Safari and Archive Utility’s setxattr("com.apple.quarantine") call to fail with EACCES, leaving the extracted application completely unquarantined so syspolicyd skips Gatekeeper and Notarization checks upon launch.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: AppleDouble (._) Restrictive ACL Extraction (deny writeextattr) (T1222.002) -> Stage 2: setxattr(com.apple.quarantine) Blocked by Kernel ACL Check (T1553.001) -> Stage 3: Gatekeeper & Lockdown Mode Bypass on App Launch (T1204.002)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Security Threat Intelligence (Jonathan Bar Or): Gatekeeper’s Achilles heel: Unearthing a macOS vulnerability (CVE-2022-42821)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/12/19/gatekeepers-achilles-heel-unearthing-a-macos-vulnerability/); [Jamf Threat Labs: Monitoring macOS Gatekeeper Bypasses & Unquarantined Execution with Endpoint Security (ESF)](https://www.jamf.com/blog/); [Apple Product Security: About the security content of macOS Ventura 13.1, Monterey 12.6.2, and Big Sur 11.7.2 (CVE-2022-42821)](https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT213532)

### CVE-2023-28252: Kaspersky GReAT & Microsoft — Windows CLFS.sys Kernel Zero-Day EoP & Nokoyawa Ransomware
- **ID:** `windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa
- **Category:** MALWARE | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a high-security courthouse (Windows Kernel Ring-0) that lets any citizen on the street (Medium Integrity User) ask the court clerk (CLFS.sys, Common Log File System) to maintain a ledger book (.blf Base Log File) stored in a public locker (C:\Users\Public\log.blf). The ledger book contains page-index numbers (SignaturesOffset and rgClients) that tell the clerk where to write inside the courthouse’s own memory, protected only by a simple math checksum (CRC32). While the ledger is sitting on disk, the attacker edits the page-index numbers to point straight at a fake instruction table (Fake CClfsContainer vtable -> ClfsEarlierLsn) and recalculates the CRC32 checksum. When the clerk reads the ledger back in, it trusts the checksum, jumps to the fake instruction table, copies the Supreme Judge’s badge (PID 4 SYSTEM EPROCESS Token) onto the attacker’s coat, and lets them unleash Nokoyawa ransomware across the building! Discovered in the wild by Kaspersky GReAT and patched by Microsoft MSRC (April 2023), CVE-2023-28252 is an actively exploited Windows Common Log File System (CLFS.sys) kernel zero-day Elevation of Privilege vulnerability used to deploy Nokoyawa ransomware. A low-privileged attacker calls CreateLogFile() to create a .blf file on disk, corrupts CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER and CClfsBaseFilePersisted offsets while forging a valid CRC32 checksum, triggers an out-of-bounds kernel write in CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock, pivots through a fake CClfsContainer vtable and ClfsEarlierLsn to overwrite the process EPROCESS Token with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, and launches nokoyawa.exe.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: Malformed Base Log File (.blf) Creation & CRC32 Forgery (T1068) -> Stage 2: CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock OOB Write & ClfsEarlierLsn Gadget (T1134.001) -> Stage 3: SYSTEM Privilege Escalation & Nokoyawa Ransomware Execution (T1486)
- **Primary Sources:** [Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist): Nokoyawa ransomware attacks use new Windows zero-day vulnerability in CLFS (CVE-2023-28252)](https://securelist.com/nokoyawa-ransomware-attacks-use-zero-day/109483/); [Zscaler ThreatLabz: Technical Analysis of Windows CLFS Zero-Day Vulnerability CVE-2023-28252 & Nokoyawa Ransomware](https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/technical-analysis-windows-clfs-zero-day-vulnerability-cve-2023-28252); [Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV: Windows Common Log File System Driver Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2023-28252)](https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-28252)

### T1078.004: Mandiant & Snowflake — UNC5537 Campaign: Infostealer Credential Replay & FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) Exfiltration
- **ID:** `snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=snowflake-unc5537-saas-extortion
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a high-security cloud storage facility (Snowflake) where the vault doors themselves are unbreakable, but several corporate tenants told the front desk: "Let our contractors walk in with just a written password, don’t ask them for a second security badge (MFA = NULL) or check what taxi (IP Network Policy) they arrived in." A thief (UNC5537) buys old boxes of stolen home-computer diaries (Lumma / RedLine / Vidar infostealer logs), searches those diaries for the word snowflakecomputing.com, walks right through the front door with a high-speed robotic inventory scanner (FROSTBITE / Rapeflake), packs gigabytes of customer ledgers into zip bags (COPY INTO @~), and carries them out. Synthesizing Mandiant’s UNC5537 investigation, Snowflake’s joint security advisory, and CISA guidance (June 2024), this scenario models how financially motivated threat actor UNC5537 breached over 165 enterprise Snowflake customer tenants without exploiting any vulnerability in Snowflake itself. The actors extracted valid corporate credentials from historical infostealer malware logs (RedLine, Vidar, LummaC2), logged into single-factor accounts lacking Multi-Factor Authentication (SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR = NULL) and Network Policies, ran the custom .NET utility FROSTBITE (Rapeflake) to enumerate schemas, and used DBeaver Ultimate to stage (COPY INTO) and download multi-gigabyte customer tables.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: INFOSTEALER CREDENTIAL REPLAY ON SINGLE-FACTOR TENANT (T1078.004) -> Stage 2: FROSTBITE (RAPEFLAKE) AUTOMATED SCHEMA RECONNAISSANCE (T1087.004) -> Stage 3: DBEAVER ULTIMATE BULK STAGE & MULTI-GB EXFILTRATION (T1530)

### T1552.005: AWS Security, Unit 42 & MITRE — EC2 Reverse-Proxy SSRF to IMDSv1 (169.254.169.254) IAM Role & S3 Exfiltration
- **ID:** `aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=aws-imdsv1-ssrf-capitalone-style
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an office mailroom clerk (EC2 Reverse Proxy / Web App) whose job is to fetch public brochures from any website address you write on a request slip (?url=...). Inside the building, however, there is an internal pneumatic tube at extension 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv1) that automatically dispenses a temporary master keycard (ASIA... STS IAM Role Credentials) to anyone sitting inside the building who asks for it, no questions asked! By writing http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ on the public request slip (SSRF), an outsider tricks the mailroom clerk into fetching the building’s master keycard and mailing a photocopy straight back to the street. Grounded in AWS Security’s IMDSv2 architecture documentation, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 cloud research, and MITRE ATT&CK T1552.005, this scenario demonstrates how a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) flaw on an Amazon EC2 instance with legacy IMDSv1 enabled (HttpTokens=optional) compromises the underlying cloud account. The attacker coerces the EC2 web service into sending an HTTP GET request to the link-local metadata IP (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<RoleName>), extracts the temporary AWS STS AccessKeyId (ASIA...), SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken, and replays them from an external machine via aws s3 sync to exfiltrate private S3 buckets.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: SSRF INJECTION TO LINK-LOCAL IMDSV1 ROLE DISCOVERY (T1190) -> Stage 2: EXTRACTION OF TEMPORARY AWS STS ROLE CREDENTIALS (ASIA...) (T1552.005) -> Stage 3: OFF-CLOUD CREDENTIAL REPLAY & S3 BUCKET SYNC EXFILTRATION (T1530)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### CVE-2024-21626: Snyk, OpenContainers & Sysdig — "Leaky Vessels" runc WORKDIR (/proc/self/fd/7) Host File-Descriptor Container Escape
- **ID:** `k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a prison guard (runc <= 1.1.11) who is escorting a new inmate (container process) into a locked isolation cell (pivot_root container filesystem). Before locking the cell door, the guard opens a clipboard folder (file descriptor 7 / fd 7) that is clipped to the main prison warden’s office hallway (/sys/fs/cgroup on the host OS). The inmate’s intake form says: "Please stand inside folder #7 (WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7)." The guard absentmindedly lets the inmate step onto the clipboard’s hallway floor before locking the cell door and snapping the clipboard shut (O_CLOEXEC)! Even though the clipboard is closed a millisecond later, the inmate’s feet (current working directory ".") are already standing in the warden’s hallway, so walking four steps backward (cd ../../../..) puts the inmate right inside the host server’s master control room. Discovered by Snyk Security Labs (Rory McNamara) and patched by OpenContainers in January 2024 ("Leaky Vessels", CVE-2024-21626), runc versions <= 1.1.11 leaked an open file descriptor (fd 7, 8, or 9) pointing to the underlying host’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory into the container initialization step. By setting WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7 in a malicious Dockerfile (or running runc exec --cwd /proc/self/fd/7), the container process changes its current working directory to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup dentry before execve() closes the file descriptor, allowing relative ../../../../etc/shadow traversal and full Kubernetes worker-node root takeover.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: RUNC CGROUP FILE DESCRIPTOR LEAK BEFORE PIVOT_ROOT (T1611) -> Stage 2: PERSISTENT HOST DENTRY ANCHOR IN CONTAINER CURRENT DIRECTORY (T1611) -> Stage 3: RELATIVE DOT-DOT TRAVERSAL TO HOST ROOTFS & KUBELET COMPROMISE (T1068)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### T1606.002: Microsoft Threat Intel, Wiz & CISA — Storm-0558: Acquired MSA Consumer Signing Key & Forged OWA/Exchange Online Tokens
- **ID:** `microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a global hotel chain (Microsoft Cloud) that runs two completely separate divisions: a casual Public Gym (Consumer MSA / Outlook.com) and a classified Diplomatic Embassy Tower (Enterprise Azure AD / Exchange Online). Each division has its own wax signet ring (cryptographic signing key) for stamping visitor passes. One day in 2021, a Public Gym printing machine crashes, and a photo of the trash bin (crash dump) accidentally includes the Public Gym’s wax signet ring (2016 MSA consumer signing key). A spy (Storm-0558) finds that ring in the crash dump and stamps a fake VIP pass claiming to be an Embassy Ambassador. When the spy hands that pass to the Embassy Tower’s mailroom guard (Exchange Online / OWA), the guard carefully checks with a magnifying glass that the wax seal came from a real Microsoft ring, yet forgets to check that a Public Gym ring is never allowed to sign an Embassy Tower pass! Synthesizing Microsoft Threat Intelligence’s technical post-mortem, Joint CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-193A, and Wiz Research (July–September 2023), China-nexus espionage actor Storm-0558 acquired an inactive 2016 Microsoft Account (MSA) consumer signing private key that had been inadvertently written into a 2021 process crash dump. By exploiting a cross-realm signature validation bug in Outlook Web Access (OWA) and Exchange Online where enterprise relying parties verified token signatures against a shared key store without checking whether the signing key belonged to the consumer (MSA) vs. enterprise (Entra ID) trust realm, Storm-0558 forged access tokens to silently exfiltrate emails from 25 organizations including government agencies.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: OFFLINE TOKEN FORGERY USING CRASH-DUMP MSA SIGNING KEY (T1552.004) -> Stage 2: CROSS-REALM VALIDATION BYPASS IN EXCHANGE ONLINE / OWA (T1606.002) -> Stage 3: SILENT OWA MAILBOX COLLECTION & CISA AA23-193A DETECTION (T1114.002)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### T1556.007: SpecterOps, Mandiant & Microsoft — Entra Connect (Azure AD Connect) MSOL_ DKM Decryption & Seamless SSO Silver Ticket
- **ID:** `azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=azure-ad-connect-pass-the-certificate
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a translator’s desk (Entra Connect / Azure AD Connect Server) that sits between a company’s local castle (On-Premises Active Directory) and its cloud fortress (Microsoft Entra ID). To keep both sides synchronized, the translator keeps a locked desk drawer (ADSync.mdf -> mms_management_agent LocalDB table) containing the master skeleton key to the local castle (MSOL_<hex> account with DCSync rights), and hangs the key to that drawer (DPAPI cryptKeySet) right under the desk! If an intruder compromises the translator’s server, they reach under the desk, unlock the drawer with the translator’s own magnifying glass (mcrypt.dll), grab the MSOL_ skeleton key to copy every secret in the local castle, including the AZUREADSSOACC$ bridge key, and forge golden passes straight into the cloud fortress. Synthesizing research by Dirk-jan Mollema (_dirkjan / AADInternals), SpecterOps, and Mandiant, this scenario demonstrates why Microsoft Entra Connect (formerly Azure AD Connect) is a critical Tier-0 hybrid identity asset. When an attacker gains local administrator privileges on the Entra Connect server (CORP-AADC01), they impersonate NT SERVICE\ADSync, query the local SQL Express ADSync database (mms_management_agent), load Entra Connect’s mcrypt.dll assembly to DPAPI-decrypt the on-premises MSOL_<hex> connector account password, use MSOL_ to execute a DCSync attack against the Domain Controller, and extract the AZUREADSSOACC$ computer account hash to forge Seamless SSO Kerberos Silver Tickets for any synced cloud user.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: QUERYING ADSYNC LOCALDB (MMS_MANAGEMENT_AGENT) BLOBS (T1003) -> Stage 2: DPAPI & MCRYPT.DLL DECRYPTION OF MSOL_ CONNECTOR PASSWORD (T1552.001) -> Stage 3: MSOL_ DCSYNC & AZUREADSSOACC$ SEAMLESS SSO CLOUD PIVOT (T1556.007)

### T1098.001: Rhino Security Labs, Datadog & AWS — IAM PassRole + Lambda CreateFunction Privilege Escalation & CloudTrail StopLogging
- **ID:** `aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=aws-cognito-iam-passrole-privesc
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a junior clerk (ci-dev-deployer) at a bank who is forbidden from opening the main vault (no iam:AttachUserPolicy permission). However, the clerk has two seemingly harmless permissions: they are allowed to build small automated mail-sorting robots (lambda:CreateFunction), and they are allowed to clip any existing employee badge onto a robot (iam:PassRole). The clerk spots the Bank President’s spare badge (LambdaAdminDeploymentRole) hanging on the wall, clips that badge onto a brand-new 5-line Python robot (metrics-health-sync-tmp), and presses the robot’s "Start" button (lambda:InvokeFunction). Wearing the President’s badge, the robot walks over to HR, promotes the junior clerk to Bank President (AdministratorAccess), and unplugs the security cameras (cloudtrail:StopLogging)! Grounded in Rhino Security Labs’ canonical AWS IAM Privilege Escalation research, Datadog Security Labs, and MITRE ATT&CK (T1098.001 / T1562.008), this scenario models one of the most common privilege escalation paths in AWS cloud environments. A compromised developer IAM user (ci-dev-deployer) lacking administrative rights abuses the intersection of iam:PassRole, lambda:CreateFunction, and lambda:InvokeFunction to create a Python Lambda function bound to a privileged service role (LambdaAdminDeploymentRole). When invoked, the Lambda function executes boto3 calls under the privileged role to attach arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess to the attacker’s IAM user and disable CloudTrail logging via cloudtrail:StopLogging.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: IAM PASSROLE & MALICIOUS LAMBDA FUNCTION CREATION (T1098.001) -> Stage 2: LAMBDA INVOCATION & ADMINISTRATORACCESS POLICY ATTACHMENT (T1098.003) -> Stage 3: CLOUDTRAIL STOPLOGGING DEFENSE EVASION (T1562.008)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### T1610: Sysdig TRT, Permiso & Unit 42 — SCARLETEEL Operation: Kubernetes Pod RCE, AWS Terraform .tfstate Theft & Pacu Pivot
- **ID:** `sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a burglar (SCARLETEEL) who slips through an open window into a small workshop annex (Kubernetes Pod in AWS EKS). The workshop annex only has keys to a hallway supply closet (S3 DevOps Bucket). However, sitting inside that supply closet is the master architectural blueprint book (terraform.tfstate) that the building’s engineers used to construct the entire corporate campus! Because the blueprint tool (Terraform) writes down the actual cleartext combination (aws_iam_access_key.attributes.secret) of every vault it builds right inside that book, reading terraform.tfstate hands the burglar the permanent master keys to the company’s main production bank vaults across the street. Discovered and analyzed by the Sysdig Threat Research Team (SCARLETEEL & SCARLETEEL 2.0), Permiso P0 Labs, and Palo Alto Unit 42, this scenario models a sophisticated cloud-native intrusion chain that pivots from a single Kubernetes container into multi-account AWS dominance. After exploiting an internet-facing workload pod in Amazon EKS, the attacker queries the worker node’s Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254), uses the node role to download terraform.tfstate from an S3 backend bucket, extracts plaintext aws_iam_access_key secret keys belonging to privileged cross-account administrators, and uses the Pacu framework to steal proprietary source code and S3 datasets.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: KUBERNETES POD RCE & NODE IMDS CREDENTIAL HARVESTING (T1190) -> Stage 2: S3 TERRAFORM STATE (.TFSTATE) PLAINTEXT SECRET EXTRACTION (T1552.001) -> Stage 3: CROSS-ACCOUNT PACU PIVOT & PROPRIETARY CODE EXFILTRATION (T1078.004)

### T1098.001: Mandiant, Wiz & Google Cloud — GCP iam.serviceAccountKeys.create & serviceAccounts.actAs Impersonation Escalation
- **ID:** `gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=gcp-service-account-hmac-key-pivot
- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a cloud office building (GCP Project) where every virtual machine comes with a default janitor robot (<project-number>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com) that was accidentally given a master key to every room in the building (roles/editor). A contractor (ci-runner service account) doesn’t have access to the financial vault (gs://corp-financial-ledger-prod), but their badge allows them to print new ID cards for any robot in the building (iam.serviceAccountKeys.create). The contractor walks up to the card printer (iam.googleapis.com), prints a brand-new JSON private key card (loot_key.json) in the name of the Editor janitor robot, puts on that card, and empties the financial vault! Synthesizing research by Mandiant (Google Cloud Threat Intelligence), Wiz Research, and Rhino Security Labs, this scenario models the classic Google Cloud Platform (GCP) IAM privilege escalation chain abusing iam.serviceAccountKeys.create (or iam.serviceAccounts.actAs) against the over-privileged Default Compute Engine Service Account (<project-number>-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com). Because GCP projects historically granted the Default Compute Service Account the broad primitive role roles/editor, any identity with project-wide Service Account Key Admin permissions can mint a persistent user-managed RSA private key JSON file for that account and inherit full read/write control over Cloud Storage (GCS) and BigQuery.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: ENUMERATING PRIVILEGED DEFAULT COMPUTE SERVICE ACCOUNT (T1087.004) -> Stage 2: MINTING USER-MANAGED RSA JSON KEY VIA CREATESERVICEACCOUNTKEY (T1098.001) -> Stage 3: IMPERSONATED EDITOR AUTHENTICATION & GCS BUCKET EXFILTRATION (T1530)

### T1539: Okta Security, Cloudflare & BeyondTrust — Support Case .har File sid Session Token Theft & Admin API Token Minting
- **ID:** `okta-har-file-session-token-hijack`

- **Category:** CLOUD_SAAS | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a bank manager (IT Super Admin) who notices a minor display glitch on their computer screen while logged into the master vault console (Okta Admin Console). To show the vendor’s helpdesk what the glitch looks like, the manager turns on a high-definition video camera (Chrome DevTools Save all as HAR with content) that films the screen, and accidentally films a close-up of the live, already-unlocked temporary master keycard (Cookie: sid=102f8a9c...) sitting on the desk! When a burglar compromises the helpdesk’s file cabinet, they grab that .har recording, 3D-print an exact copy of the sid keycard within 30 minutes, walk past both the password guard and the MFA guard because the session is already open, and try to mint a permanent master key (SSWS API Token). Synthesizing official post-mortems from Okta Security, Cloudflare SIRT, BeyondTrust, and 1Password (October–November 2023), this scenario models how a threat actor breached Okta’s customer support case-management system and harvested unsanitized browser HTTP Archive (.har) files uploaded by customer administrators. Because .har files record raw HTTP headers including active Cookie: sid=<session_token> values from post-MFA administrative sessions, the attacker replayed the stolen sid cookies from commercial VPN nodes to hijack active Okta Super Admin sessions, create backdoor accounts, and mint permanent SSWS API tokens, until real-time SIRT rules detected a single externalSessionId roaming across different Autonomous Systems (ASNs).
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: EXTRACTING LIVE SID SESSION COOKIES FROM SUPPORT .HAR FILES (T1539) -> Stage 2: REPLAYING SID COOKIE TO BYPASS MFA IN OKTA ADMIN CONSOLE (T1550.004) -> Stage 3: MINTING PERSISTENT SSWS API TOKENS & SIRT SESSION REVOCATION (T1098.001)

### T1190: Kaseya VSA MSP Zero-Day & REvil MsMpEng.exe Side-Loading (CVE-2021-30116)
- **ID:** `kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=kaseya-vsa-revil-cve-2021-30116
- **Category:** SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine an IT support company that holds master remote-control switches for 1,500 local businesses. A gang of extortionists tricks the main switchboard into accepting a fake master badge, sends an emergency "security update" down the wire to every business at once, tells each computer’s real security guard to go to sleep, and dresses the thief up in an old security guard uniform (MsMpEng.exe) to lock every file. Over the July 2021 holiday weekend, REvil exploited CVE-2021-30116 against internet-facing Kaseya VSA servers run by Managed Service Providers (MSPs). Bypassing authentication on /dl.asp, they uploaded agent.crt and triggered a Kaseya Agent Procedure across all managed endpoints that disabled Windows Defender, decoded agent.crt via certutil.exe, and used DLL side-loading (MsMpEng.exe + mpsvc.dll) to execute REvil ransomware.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: Stage 1: Kaseya VSA /dl.asp Authentication Bypass & agent.crt Upload (T1190) -> Stage 2: Stage 2: Kaseya Agent Procedure Disabling Defender & Decoding agent.exe (T1562.001) -> Stage 3: Stage 3: MsMpEng.exe DLL Side-Loading of REvil Ransomware (mpsvc.dll) (T1574.002)
- **Primary Sources:** [Microsoft Win32 API Reference: CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw); [Microsoft Sysinternals: Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering); [Elastic Security Labs: Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs)

### T1190: FortiManager fgfmsd Unauthenticated API RCE ("FortiJump" CVE-2024-47575 / UNC5820)
- **ID:** `fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=fortimanager-fgd-jump-cve-2024-47575
- **Category:** ZERO_DAY_APPLIANCES | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine the central headquarters that manages 500 branch bank vaults. Headquarters has a dedicated phone line (Port 541) meant only for branch vaults calling in to sync their combinations. Due to a flaw, headquarters checks that the caller has a laminated ID card, but never checks if the serial number on the card actually belongs to the bank. A thief calls in with a fake serial number, gets patched straight through to the master archive clerk (rcs_checkout), and downloads the combinations to all 500 branch vaults. Tracked by Mandiant as UNC5820 beginning in June 2024 and disclosed by Fortinet in October 2024 (FG-IR-24-423), CVE-2024-47575 ("FortiJump", CVSS 9.8) is a missing authentication vulnerability in the FortiGate-to-FortiManager (fgfmsd) protocol on TCP port 541. By presenting a self-signed or arbitrary certificate and registering an unknown serial number, an unauthenticated attacker reaches internal API handlers like rcs_checkout, injects shell commands as root, and steals /var/fwclient containing the configurations and password hashes of every managed FortiGate.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: Stage 1: Unauthenticated FGFM TLS Handshake & Rogue Device Registration (TCP/541) (T1190) -> Stage 2: Stage 2: FGFM put_json / rcs_checkout Command Injection as Root (T1059.004) -> Stage 3: Stage 3: Exfiltration of Managed FortiGate Configurations (/var/fwclient & globaldb) (T1005)

### T1542.003: BlackLotus UEFI Bootkit Baton Drop Secure Boot Bypass (CVE-2022-21894)
- **ID:** `blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894`
- **Canonical URL:** https://attackexplorer.org/scenarios/blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894
- **Simulator Deep Link:** https://attackexplorer.org/?scenario=blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-cve-2022-21894
- **Category:** KERNEL_FIRMWARE_BYOVD | **Severity:** CRITICAL
- **Overview:** Imagine a high-security building where every morning at 6:00 AM, a robot checks that the front-door guard has a genuine badge signed by the mayor before letting the guard turn on the security cameras. A burglar brings an retired guard from two years ago, who still holds a genuine badge signed by the mayor, because the mayor forgot to put that old badge on the "revoked" list, and hands the retired guard a rigged clipboard (BCD) that tricks them into leaving the security cameras unplugged for the rest of the day. Analyzed by ESET and the subject of a joint NSA/CISA advisory in 2023, BlackLotus is an 80-kilobyte C/Assembly UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing UEFI Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. Using a "Bring Your Own Vulnerable Bootloader" (BYOVB) technique, it drops older, legitimately signed bootmgfw.efi, hvloader.efi, and winload.efi binaries onto the EFI System Partition and exploits CVE-2022-21894 ("Baton Drop") to disable Code Integrity in early boot, turn off BitLocker and HVCI, and load an unsigned kernel rootkit.
- **Stages (3):** Stage 1: Stage 1: EFI System Partition Staging & MOK NVRAM Variable Tampering (T1542.003) -> Stage 2: Stage 2: "Baton Drop" BCD Argument Truncation Exploit (CVE-2022-21894) (T1562.001) -> Stage 3: Stage 3: Disabling BitLocker / HVCI & Deploying Unsigned Ring-0 Kernel Driver (T1068)
